title: The vigil and the crowning
body: Ailean keeps watch by the seven fires for seven nights, fasting, a night for each coal. On the eighth night the coals are cold, and Caoran comes into the grove with the Tuath Dè about him. He names Ailean Rìgh Chlann nan Dè, king of the godkin, and puts into him the power that was in the coals. Of that power Ailean tells no one while he lives.

title: Coinneach follows his brother north
body: Coinneach mac Shuibhne, unable to wait out a year of silence, sets off after his brother with a sack of oatcake and a skin of buttermilk, following the roads he judges Ailean must have taken toward the grove of Doire ghlas.

title: The camp beyond the oaks
body: Coinneach comes within sight of the seven fires at Doire ghlas and finds he cannot cross into the ring of oaks. Coimhdeach na Fine allows him to camp at the tree-line and no nearer, and he keeps his own vigil there through the seven nights of his brother's watch.

title: Voices heard on the fifth night
body: On the fifth night of the vigil Coinneach hears, low under the sound of the fires, what he takes for voices, one of them shaped almost like his brother's speech though fallen into a rhythm Ailean never used. He never swears to more than that he heard something.

title: The grove fills with light
body: On the eighth night, when the seven fires go dark together, Coinneach watches the grove of Doire ghlas fill with a light that is not firelight, and sees shapes moving among the oaks. His feet will not carry him past the tree-line to follow them.

title: The six pots left cold
body: At dawn the six pots that carried Ailean's fires north are found lying empty on the leaves of Doire ghlas, their turf lids scattered, and the pale stone that held the seventh coal lies among them, giving no light but warm to the touch.

title: Coinneach finds his brother warm at dawn
body: Ailean walks out of the grove at morning and catches his stumbling brother by the arm. Coinneach feels a warmth in it like a hearthstone long after the fire is swept, and knows before any word is said that the night has changed his brother.

title: "They named me king"
body: Ailean tells his brother only this much of the night in the grove: that he has been named king. He says nothing of who named him, of what a king might be king of, or of what was put into him, and Coinneach asks no further, having seen enough from outside the trees.

title: The brothers turn south
body: Ailean gathers the six empty pots onto his shoulder-pole, leaves the pale seventh stone lying uncovered among the leaves of Doire ghlas, and sets out south with his brother, never lighting the six fires again.

title: Ailean passes Na Glinn Àrda
body: Ailean walks south past the households of Clann na Ceiste in Na Glinn Àrda without turning aside to any hearth, though he has kin enough among them to be fed and questioned there.

title: Eleven kin walk south with him
body: Households of Clann na Ceiste near Na Glinn Àrda leave byre and field to follow Ailean south, eleven in all, none able afterward to give a better reason than a feeling not to be argued with. The king shares out Coinneach's sack among them on the road.

title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings
body: Ailean Mòr, crowned in the grove, comes down to the hill where Dùn ìseal now stands and takes it, and brings the households of the valleys about it under his hand: the first kingdom of the godkin. How he won, none who stood against him could say. He throws up the hill's first ring of bank. He is king from that day until his death, and gives the kingship to no one. With him opens the eldest of the spoken king-lists, afterwards called Rìghrean na Cloiche, which names those who held the hill; it gives no lengths of reign, and it is older than the name Dia-thìrich.

title: The bare ring in the frost
body: Twice on the road south the company sleeps in the open, and both mornings the frost that silvers the field leaves a bare, warm ring the size of a sleeping man where Ailean lay, as it did at his feet in the grove.

title: Coinneach keeps the first telling
body: Walking south behind his brother, Coinneach turns over what little he saw from outside the ring of oaks and fits it into an account he is careful never to swell beyond what he truly witnessed, the seed of the telling Clann na Ceiste keep of the seven nights.

title: The lad who brought the water
body: The knapper's son of Dùn ìseal is sent to the hill's crown with water for the man who has just taken it unopposed, and is asked his name and whether the spear he carries is his father's best. Told to take it home and to tell his father the king will want a great many more.

title: The valleys come in to the hill
body: Through the first year the households of the valleys about Dùn ìseal come in to the king one after another, unsummoned, bringing hides, pots, and whatever else they judge fitting, and with their gifts their grazing and their old quarrels, for a telling to be held over them.

title: The first judgement on the hill
body: Two households of Dùn ìseal bring before the king a strip of pasture each has claimed for a generation. He asks one question, of whose cattle grazed it before the boundary stone was last moved, and gives the strip back in a sentence. Neither household ever brings the matter before him again.

title: The king's order to the flint-pit
body: The flint-pit behind the houses of Dùn ìseal is set, on the king's own word, to cut spearheads by the score rather than as they are needed, the first order of its kind on the hill. The knapper's son is set to the work alongside his father before that year's leaves are down.

title: The warmth with no fire
body: In the first hard winter on the hill, a girl of Dùn ìseal stands near the king's own untended fire at night and finds herself warmed through though no flame burns close enough to account for it. She keeps the telling to herself for years before it is believed.

title: The line of the bank pegged in the snow
body: In the depth of the same winter the king walks the crown of Dùn ìseal setting ash pegs with his own hand, marking a line that takes in the old byres and ground for houses not yet built. The households break the frozen turf along it through the worst of the frost.

title: Flint tools finish the bank's ditch
body: When the antler mattocks digging the new ditch at Dùn ìseal blunt faster than they can be sharpened in the frost, the flint-pit sends up scrapers of worked stone to finish the work, so that the hill's first bank is cut as much with flint as with iron.

title: Muireall and Gormshuil brought to the hill
body: As the frost breaks a small company comes down from Na Glinn Àrda to Dùn ìseal: Muireall, the king's wife, and Gormshuil, his young daughter, with a few kin and hands beside them. The hill, which had thought the king had no household of his own, falls quiet to let them through the new gate.

title: Dòmhnall born within the new bank
body: A son is born to Muireall inside the finished bank of Dùn ìseal, the first of the king's children to draw breath on ground he holds, and the hill takes it as a settled thing that the king has come to stay among them.

title: A spearhead given for nothing
body: The knapper cuts a spearhead finer than any he has made that year, for no order and no payment, and sends it up to the king's fire on the birth of the king's son. He will not say why, only that the giving seemed owed.

title: The bank of Dùn ìseal
body: The first earthwork is raised on the hill at Dùn ìseal: a single bank and ditch, enclosing room for some forty houses. It is the oldest defended place of the hill-folk.

title: Gormshuil set to keep the gate
body: A child of eight, Gormshuil is given the gate of the new bank to watch, and takes to naming every face and dog on the hill so her father will have someone to tell him at evening what the day brought. The habit holds her the rest of her life.

title: Fearchar born on the hill
body: A second son is born to the king within the new bank of Dùn ìseal and named Fearchar; he is the first of the king's children to open his eyes on the hill itself, and will hold it for his father in his time.

title: Beathag Ruadh of the Red Hill
body: Beathag Ruadh holds the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands. With her opens a second spoken list, kept in the west. The Red Hill list and the list of the Stone Kings make no mention of each other until late in both.

title: Word of the red hill's woman
body: A salt-fish trader carries word up to Dùn ìseal of a woman holding a red hill on the shore of the great lake in her own right, answering to no king. Gormshuil asks her father whether it means trouble; he tells her trouble comes from nearer at hand.

title: Muireall's dying words
body: In her last two nights Muireall speaks to her daughter of small things, a comb, a debt owed, and warns that her youngest son Fearchar has a temper that will want watching before it finds him trouble he cannot talk his way out of.

title: The king hears three cases the day Muireall is buried
body: Two days after Muireall is put in the ground the king comes in from the valleys, stands by the mound, then goes into the hearing-house and gives judgement on three waiting cases before dark. He does not speak her name again where any ear can catch it.

title: Gormshuil nic Ailein
body: Gormshuil nic Ailein, the king's daughter, holds the hill of Dùn ìseal for her father while he rides beyond it, and the list names her second of the Stone Kings; she is the first woman named in any list on Dia-thìr. She was born before the grove, and has none of the long years. One deed is told of her: in a hard winter she moves the herds of Dùn ìseal down to the warm springs and loses none.

title: The drive to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
body: With the hardest winter in living memory emptying the byres and the king three valleys off, Gormshuil drives the standing herds two days through drifted snow to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, walking the whole way herself so no beast's fodder is spent on a rider. She loses none.

title: The two fingers that never bent again
body: Gormshuil comes off the winter drive with two fingers of her left hand frozen stiff, and wears a glove over them in company from that year to her death without ever speaking of how they were got.

title: The king weds Sorcha
body: Ailean takes a second wife, Sorcha, a woman of the valleys younger than his own eldest daughter, and the hill notes the matter and does not remark on it aloud, as it has grown used to doing with the king's household.

title: Coinneach's counsel on the bank
body: Gormshuil tells Coinneach that her father does not age while she has begun to grey. He tells her what he saw the night the fires went out in the grove, and counsels her to keep from asking her father what it cost him, as he has kept from asking these thirty years.

title: Somhairle born
body: Sorcha bears the king a son, Somhairle, in the thirty-eighth year after the grove, the first child of Sorcha's line to be counted among those got after the grove.

title: Beathag Ruadh dies on An Cnoc Ruadh
body: Beathag Ruadh, who held An Cnoc Ruadh by the lake before any of the valleys came in to the king, dies an old woman in her own hall, unsworn and unbeaten; her household keeps the palisade after her and the lake shore does not change its ways for her going.

title: Iain Dubh born
body: A second son of Sorcha's, Iain Dubh, is born to the king on the hill, the youngest of Ailean's children to be reckoned among Rìghrean na Cloiche in his turn.

title: Coinneach dies, Sloinneadh a' Chlachair passed whole
body: Coinneach mac Shuibhne dies an old man, the first teller of the king's deeds, having taught Gormshuil Sloinneadh a' Chlachair word for word as Coimhdeach na Fine gave it in the grove. She is, after her father, the second on the hill to carry the whole of it.

title: The grandchildren take the king for her son
body: Gormshuil's own grandchildren, seeing the king young at the gate each autumn beside a bent grey grandmother, take him for her son rather than her father, and she lets the mistake stand rather than make them carry a harder truth too young.

title: Gormshuil's deathbed question
body: On the second night of her dying Gormshuil asks her father whether it hurts to stay young. He does not answer her in words, and says her name once instead, the way a man says a name he does not expect to say again.

title: Gormshuil dies
body: Gormshuil nic Ailein dies an old woman of eighty-one, the king's eldest daughter and second of Rìghrean na Cloiche. He sits by her a night and a day and helps lift the turf over her with his own hands, as he did for no one since Muireall.

title: The hill understands na Bliadhnachan Fada
body: Watching Gormshuil, who carried her father's stubbornness and stillness but not his years, put into the ground beside a father who looks her grandson's age, the hill understands at last that na Bliadhnachan Fada are the grove's alone, and pass to no child got before it.

title: Dòmhnall takes the hill
body: Dòmhnall Clachach, seventy-four and looking a young man still, takes up the hearing-house his half-sister held since the grove, and says he supposes he had better learn to count who comes and goes, since no one is left who learned it from the start as she did.

title: Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones
body: Dòmhnall Clachach, a son of the king and third of the Stone Kings, holds the hill after Gormshuil and sets marker stones along the valley below it to part the grazing of Dùn ìseal from its neighbours'. Some stand yet, and are argued over yet.

title: The old men disagree at the setting of the stones
body: As Dòmhnall Clachach walks the eastern boundary with his stone-setters, the old men of neighbouring households cannot agree, standing on the very ground, where a line has always run, for the becks have shifted and their memories have not moved with them.

title: A grazing quarrel judged by the stones
body: Two households dispute a marker on the eastern slope, each swearing it stands to the wrong side of the old line. Dòmhnall Clachach settles it from his own memory of the setting, and both sides go home certain, for the first time, that a stone remembers better than a grandfather.

title: Dòmhnall doubts his own stones
body: Walking home from the judgement at the marker, Dòmhnall Clachach understands that he has settled the quarrel only because his own long memory outlasts any old man's, and that the stones, once he is gone from the hill, will have no one left to ask which story is true.

title: Griogar's household turns back the king's riders
body: In a valley to the north-west a hard old man called Griogar meets two of the king's riders with spears and no parley, the first household in years to refuse the king's word outright rather than simply keep clear of it.

title: The first named storm
body: A tempest comes so great that the eldest spoken king-lists give it a name. The name is lost; only the memory of the naming remains.

title: The shell road broken
body: The storm breaks the shell causeway of Seann Warr in three places and floods the marsh behind it with lake water. The Seann-Dhaoine do not mend it, and the broken ends may be seen still.

title: Storm damage within the bank of Dùn ìseal
body: The first named storm strips the thatch from six houses of Dùn ìseal and levels a seventh to its footings. Dòmhnall Clachach spends the night holding roofs down with rope and his own weight, and the hill loses its summer hay and two sheds of the flint-pit, but no one within the bank.

title: Word of the broken causeway reaches Dùn ìseal
body: Traders driven from their usual road by flooded fords bring Dòmhnall Clachach word that the shell causeway of Seann Warr stands broken in three places, and that the Seann-Dhaoine have watched it stay broken through a winter without coming out to mend it.

title: Labhrainn refuses the boundary of his western fence
body: Labhrainn, elder of an old household on the western slope, refuses the line his own father stood by at its setting, the first quarrel in Dòmhnall Clachach's time that is fought not over ground but over a settling that no longer needs an old man's word to stand.

title: Dòmhnall sits an evening with Labhrainn
body: After judging against him, Dòmhnall Clachach rides out to Labhrainn's byre and sits a whole evening over the household's own brewing, asking not about the stone but the ground itself, and gives the old man back in listening something the stones had quietly taken from him.

title: Fearchar Bacach lamed in Griogar's valley
body: Riding with a dozen men against the household that turned back his riders, Ailean Mòr's son Fearchar takes a spear through the thigh that will not heal straight, though the wound should by any ordinary reckoning have killed him.

title: Somhairle asks to live among Clann na Ceiste
body: Somhairle, a son of Ailean Mòr some hundred and sixty years old and looking fifteen, asks his father for no land and no herds, only leave to live among the households of Na Glinn Àrda and be counted a single mouth at a single hearth.

title: Somhairle tells Dòmhnall why he wants no share
body: Visiting his brother in Na Glinn Àrda, Dòmhnall Clachach is told that Somhairle wants to be believed when he names whose son follows whose, once the kin have grown too many for any one hearth to hold the account, and that a man who holds land judges his own kin differently.

title: The chair of woven birch is built for Fearchar
body: The household carpenters of Dùn ìseal build Fearchar Bacach a chair of woven birch with long carrying-poles, unasked, so that he need no longer hide the leg that never set straight, and he takes to being carried with something like relief.

title: Uisdean born on An Cnoc Ruadh
body: A son is born by the lake shore to a household of An Cnoc Ruadh's holding line and named Uisdean; the watch on the palisade marks his birth with a fire on the point, as it marks every birth in that hall.

title: Fearchar Bacach
body: Fearchar Bacach, the lame, a son of the king lamed in his father's wars, holds Dùn ìseal under the king after the storm and after Dòmhnall Clachach, and is carried to the gatherings in a chair of woven birch. He is the first ruler on Dia-thìr remembered for a hurt.

title: Dòmhnall asks his father for the north
body: At a gathering below Dùn ìseal, Dòmhnall Clachach asks Ailean Mòr for ground still unsettled rather than the hill he has held a hundred and fifty years. His father grants him the north and no guidance in how to keep it.

title: Fearchar Bacach holds Dùn ìseal as Dòmhnall rides north
body: Dòmhnall Clachach leaves Dùn ìseal with a company of twelve, and the hill takes his brother Fearchar, already sitting its judgements from the chair of birch, for its holder without a word of dispute.

title: Uisdean Mòr takes An Cnoc Ruadh
body: Uisdean, five-and-twenty, takes up the holding of An Cnoc Ruadh on the western lake shore after those before him, an old line owing nothing to Dùn ìseal or to any king of the hill-folk.

title: Uilleam Faire born on An Cnoc Ruadh
body: A boatwright's son is born on the lake shore in the twelfth year of Uisdean's holding, and grows up believing, as every child of that hill does, that the water below it has always belonged to his own people alone.

title: The households dig the ditch across the neck
body: Every household of An Cnoc Ruadh turns out to cut the ditch across the low saddle of ground where the hill's rise meets the land, and to raise the oak palisade on the spoil bank behind it.

title: Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill
body: Uisdean Mòr, second of the Red Hill list, digs a ditch across the neck of the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands and sets a palisade on it. In his time the palisade burns twice and is twice rebuilt.

title: Uisdean tells the watch why the wall stands
body: Walking the palisade by night with the young Uilleam Faire, Uisdean speaks of na Bliadhnachan Fada of the king and of the valleys brought in to the south and east, and does not say whether An Cnoc Ruadh will swear when its turn comes.

title: The king's company camps unannounced on the shore
body: The king comes west along the lake shore with some two hundred spears at the end of a summer, camps below the hill, and sends up no word of his business to Uisdean or to any of An Cnoc Ruadh's households.

title: The first burning of the palisade
body: On the last watch before dawn the new palisade catches along its whole length at once in a low, dark, shining flame that no one on the wall can trace to any torch or spark. The hill beats it out by morning with lake water and green hides.

title: Uisdean rebuilds with green oak
body: Rather than wait out a season for seasoned timber, Uisdean sets the households to rebuilding the palisade at once with green oak cut from his own hill, against every carpenter's word of how badly it will burn.

title: The king's spearmen trade through the winter
body: Neither striking camp nor pressing nearer the wall, the king's company fishes the shallows and mends its gear through the winter, and trades salted fish and small goods with households of the hill who find it easier than the long carry round the lake.

title: Reothadh an Rìgh
body: In the early days of an t-Ògmhios, when the year should long since have been past any frost, a single clear night puts a white rime on the whole shore. The hill's old women name it from that morning Reothadh an Rìgh.

title: The Red Hill bends the knee
body: Ailean Mòr comes west to the Red Hill, where the palisade of Uisdean Mòr has twice burned. Uisdean comes down to the lake shore and kneels to him. The Red Hill keeps its own holders and its own list, and swears to the king and not to Dùn ìseal; so neither list names the other.

title: The second burning of the palisade
body: On the night of Reothadh an Rìgh the green oak takes in the same low, dark flame as before, and burns in less time than seasoned wood had, leaving nothing standing for the households to save.

title: Uilleam throws the water and never learns whose fire it was
body: Uilleam Faire is first to the second fire with a hide-skin of water, and throws it into the worst of the blaze without saving a hand's-breadth of the wall. He carries the question of whose fire it was the rest of his life.

title: The king's company departs east
body: Within the month of Uisdean's swearing the king's company strikes its tents and goes back east the way it came, and does not return to the lake shore.

title: Dùghall first walks the whole road to the shore
body: Dùghall, nine years old, is let walk the whole three days down to the Seann-Dhaoine's shore with his father for the first time, rather than being turned back with the pack-ponies at the last ridge. He learns the trade is carried by gesture alone, in silence kept on both sides.

title: Mòrag born to Dòmhnall Clachach
body: A daughter is born to Dòmhnall Clachach in the north country he was given, and is named Mòrag; she is the first of the king's grandchildren to carry na Bliadhnachan Fada, and grows up hard-handed among people who call her father only the stone-cutter's son.

title: The palisade raised a third time in seasoned oak
body: With no company camped below to hurry the choosing of timber, An Cnoc Ruadh rebuilds its wall a third time in properly seasoned oak. It never burns again in Uilleam Faire's lifetime.

title: Dùn ìseal's reciters tell the swearing fuller than An Cnoc Ruadh's own list
body: Word of Uisdean's kneeling reaches Dùn ìseal, whose reciters tell it with the fire, the frost and the shingle scene kept whole, fuller than An Cnoc Ruadh's own spare list ever names it. An Cnoc Ruadh never quarrels with their telling.

title: Dùghall's father gives up asking
body: Dùghall's father tells his son that he tried, once, as a young man, to learn a Seann-Dhaoine word for the goods they traded, and was met with a courtesy that would not be moved. He has not asked again in forty years, and tells Dùghall which questions the shore means to answer.

title: The road passes to Dùghall
body: Dùghall's father, too heavy in the knees for the bog-causeway, hands the whole carrying road to his son. Dùghall walks it alone that year with a string of ponies his in all but the naming, three days down to the shore and three days back.

title: Strokes on the midden stones
body: The Seann-Dhaoine begin to cut single strokes on flat stones set at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household. The strokes are not the script. They are simpler: a mark, and then another.

title: The strokes on the midden stones are first counted
body: Dùghall, three-and-twenty, notices that the flat stones set at the edge of one household's midden carry cut strokes, one or two to a stone, and that their number has grown by a few since he first began to notice them. He can get no answer to what they are, by word or by gesture.

title: Dùghall carries the question home unanswered
body: Dùghall tells his father what he has seen at the midden's edge. His father says he saw the same stones himself, years before, and had already judged them a question the shore did not mean to answer, and had stopped asking it.

title: Uisdean Mòr dies on An Cnoc Ruadh
body: Uisdean dies in his own bed on the hill in his eighty-seventh year, two-and-twenty years after the swearing, having outlived the fire, the frost and the king's two hundred spears.

title: The counting of the dead begins
body: The Seann-Dhaoine, whoever they were, who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin, begin to keep count of their dead. They keep it before ever there were Dia-thìrich to take up the custom.

title: A household mourns behind a wall of turf
body: Dùghall, come down to the shore in his sixty-seventh year, wakes in the night to low voices shaped like no ordinary talk, and to boats kept ashore past their hour. He does not go out while it lasts, having learned from the hill's own griefs not to.

title: A fresh stroke is cut beneath an old one
body: The morning after the low voices, Dùghall finds a second stroke cut fresh beneath the single old one on the newest of the midden stones, and understands, all at once, that the Seann-Dhaoine mark the going of their own dead the way a hill household marks a grave.

title: Dùghall counts every ridge on the shore
body: Dùghall walks the whole shore that morning and finds every household keeps its own ridge of stones the same way, some bearing a single stroke, some bearing more than he can easily count. He carries the understanding home and tells his father, who is glad, at the last, to have the answer he had stopped seeking.

title: Dùghall keeps the counting stones from his sons
body: Dùghall says nothing more of the midden stones to his sons as they take up the road at his shoulder, judging that each will come to the ridge himself in his own year, as he had. He judges rightly.

title: Dùghall takes his grandson down for the last time
body: One-and-seventy, and carrying the road no more himself, Dùghall takes his eldest son's boy down to the shore, both understanding without saying so that it is his last going. He finds two houses fallen roofless and fewer threads of smoke than he has ever counted there before.

title: The grandson counts the ridge and loses the count
body: Dùghall sets his grandson to count the stones of the oldest ridge, and the boy loses the count twice among stones fallen and half-sunk in the turf. Dùghall tells him it is no bad thing to meet a count a man cannot finish, if the count is an honest one.

title: Dùghall trades for less on his last shore
body: Dùghall trades what hides he carried for less than the same weight once brought, and walks the three days home with his grandson bearing, unknowing, the whole weight of what the old man had carried down that road alone for two-and-sixty years.

title: Dùghall dies on the hill
body: Dùghall Ceannaiche dies on the hill that winter, an old man by any hill reckoning, and it is his grandson who takes up the packs the next summer and walks south alone, counting the midden stones before he trades a single hide, as the old man had taught him.

title: The tally wall of Seann Warr
body: At the eastern Seann Warr the counting stones are built into a wall, each cut with its strokes, some three thousand strokes in all. The wall grows for many lifetimes.

title: The king rides east with Somhairle to Seann Warr
body: The king summons his son down from Na Glinn Àrda and rides the coast road east to Seann Warr with a small company. Somhairle, three hundred and fifty-one years old and near two hundred years among Clann na Ceiste, sees the shore he has only ever heard recited.

title: Somhairle first sees Balla nan Stràc
body: At the midden's edge of Seann Warr, Somhairle walks the whole length of the counting stones with his father and finds them built into a wall past any easy counting, the oldest courses run together into a single grey weight of strokes.

title: The king's stillness at the wall
body: The king stands a long while at the oldest of the tally stones with his hand flat against it, and tells Somhairle only that the wall has stood longer than the bank at Dùn ìseal, and perhaps longer than the grove. He says no more of it that day.

title: Somhairle sets Balla nan Stràc in the Line
body: Somhairle adds his first telling of his own to Sloinneadh a' Chlachair: the wall at Seann Warr, some three thousand strokes, grown over many lifetimes. It is the first fact he ever sets down unaided, and he keeps it carefully all his life.

title: The count at Seann Tarr
body: The counting comes to Seann Tarr in the north-east. There the stones are cut with strokes in fives and set in the floor of a house, and the house is lived in over its own dead.

title: Somhairle finds the house over the dead at Seann Tarr
body: Sent north on a grazing dispute, Somhairle walks down to Seann Tarr and finds a household living in a long low house whose floor is paved with dressed slabs cut with strokes in fives. He does not enter, and sets the custom down without asking after it.

title: A carrier brings word the strokes run thick
body: A carrier of hides tells Somhairle at a ford, in passing, that the tally stones are cut thicker that year than any season he has known, and thicker at all three shores at once. Somhairle rides to Seann Warr and Seann Tarr within the month and finds it true.

title: The bad years in the counts
body: The tally stones at Seann Warr, Seann Tarr and Seann Chwen thicken together: more strokes to each stone, more stones to each course. Death comes on three coasts at once. What it was the strokes do not tell.

title: The king's one visit to the wall
body: The king rides to Seann Warr with a small company and walks Balla nan Stràc alone, his hand against the newest stone for the better part of a morning. Asked by his son what he saw, he answers only, "A people counting," and speaks of it to no one again.

title: Somhairle sets the thickening in the Line
body: Somhairle records the king's visit to the wall in the fewest words the Line will bear: that the king stood long before it and, asked what he saw, said only that he had seen a people counting. He adds no explanation of his own.

title: The half-cut stone of Seann Chwen
body: At the Seann Chwen near Cuan dhearg the last tally stone is left half-cut: two strokes finished, a third begun and forsaken. The chisel marks stop in mid-groove.

title: Somhairle finds Clach nan Dà Stràc at Seann Chwen
body: Word of an unfinished stone reaches Na Glinn Àrda, and Somhairle rides two days south to Seann Chwen, quieter than either shore he knew. He finds the newest tally stone left with two strokes finished and a third abandoned mid-groove, the chisel marks stopped clean.

title: The last smoke seen at Seann Tarr
body: The carrier who first brought word of the thickening finds Seann Tarr's house over the dead standing open and cold, its hearth unlit, the household gone without any sign of where. Somhairle rides down the following spring and finds the whole shore silent.

title: The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent
body: After the half-cut stone no work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and their script is cut no more. How they ended no telling knows.

title: Somhairle rides the three shores in one circuit
body: In a single season, the first any reciter has made the round, Somhairle rides from Seann Warr to Seann Tarr and down to Seann Chwen and finds all three the same: middens grown over, boats rotted on their keels, turf houses softening back into the ground.

title: Somhairle sets down the Silence
body: Somhairle enters the shortest of his four tellings in the Line: that after Clach nan Dà Stràc no work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated, their middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and how they ended, the telling does not know.

title: The hill-folk find the coasts wholly empty
body: By this year no hill trader who once walked the three shores still finds a fire lit on any of them. The households who might have answered a knock are themselves gone, and carriers give the roads over to shores that no longer answer.

title: Somhairle weds Cairistìona
body: Somhairle marries Cairistìona of Na Glinn Àrda, a shepherding household's daughter of no house of Clann na Ceiste, before both their fires at the turn of the year. He sets nothing of the wedding itself in the Line, judging it a thing that belongs to the man and not to the telling.

title: Word of Beathan's birth reaches the river households
body: News that Somhairle and Cairistìona have a son, Beathan, and that the boy will be kept among Clann na Ceiste in the high pastures rather than brought to the hill, travels down every settled valley by the ordinary traffic of drovers and salt-carriers. It reaches Iain mac Fhearchair's household on the Abhainn naomh the same week as the shearing.

title: The hill-folk of the upper Abhainn naomh first say Seann Skell
body: Iain mac Fhearchair's generation on the river inherits, without ever deciding it as a household, the custom of naming the Seann-Dhaoine's old places with the plain word for old set before them. Seann Dunn, Seann Chwen and Seann Skell pass into ordinary speech as though no other names had ever been possible.

title: The old names kept
body: The hill-folk keep the names of the Seann-Dhaoine places and set before them only their own word for 'old': Seann Dunn, Seann Chwen, Seann Skell and the rest. They turn nothing into their own tongue, and the roots of those names are not understood.

title: Iain forbids his household the tower before any of them have seen it
body: Iain mac Fhearchair, recalling a single visit to the coast as a young man, tells his daughter Marsaili and the rest of his household that no good comes of taking up what the Seann-Dhaoine left lying, and names the tower at the harbour's mouth as a thing never to be entered, years before the household has any plan of settling near it.

title: Three river households crowd one bend
body: Grazing on the middle Abhainn naomh, held by one household in Iain's father's day, now feeds three grown from it, and the quarrels over the bend grow more frequent than the grass allows for. Iain begins to speak of the empty coast as a way out of them.

title: Iain calls the household to the coast
body: On a dark-half evening Iain mac Fhearchair tells his household plainly that he means to move it to the empty harbour at Seann Skell before another winter turns, judging a shore with good landing and no claimant better than another forty years of quarrelling over the river bend.

title: The old landings taken up
body: Families of the hill-folk come down the Abhainn naomh and settle in the empty river harbour at Seann Skell, using the old mole and mending none of it. They are not known to have dwelt by the water before.

title: Eleven souls come down the Abhainn naomh
body: Iain mac Fhearchair's household, eleven souls with ox-carts and what beasts they can drive, follows the Abhainn naomh two days further than any of them has gone, and comes out above the tide to find the harbour at Seann Skell standing exactly as the traders had always described it: empty, the old mole running into the flood, the tower blind-walled by the water.

title: Iain marks the ground and forbids the tower again
body: Before the household sleeps its first night at the harbour, Iain walks the ground himself and sets a line of stones marking where a house may be built and where it must not, keeping every wall a household's length from the nearest standing Seann-Dhaoine wall and the whole camp further still from the tower.

title: The household mends the mole with stone it did not take
body: The household repairs the landward stretch of the old mole with stone gathered fresh from the shore, never lifting a stone already laid by the Seann-Dhaoine, a distinction Iain draws carefully and his children keep after him without ever quite putting into words.

title: A winter storm breaks the seaward mole
body: In the first days of an Fhaoilleach a storm out of the west drives the tide higher up the shingle than any of the household remembers from their river years, and breaks the oldest, untouched stretch of the mole, scattering its stones along the shore.

title: Iain refuses to build with the broken stone
body: Two of Iain's sons-in-law argue that stone the sea itself has thrown down is no longer bound by the household's rule against taking up Seann-Dhaoine work. Iain refuses them, holding that the storm's breaking gives the household no claim the storm did not also give, and the mole is mended instead with new-quarried stone.

title: The mole stands whole again
body: After two summers of quarrying and hauling stone down from the higher ground, the mended mole stands sheltered end to end, and no household on that shore again seriously argues for lifting a Seann-Dhaoine stone to lay it elsewhere.

title: The first hill-folk boats put out from Seann Skell
body: Tearlach mac Ghilleonain and two of Iain's grandsons build the first boats the harbour has held since it was last worked, small hide craft trusted for the first time to open tide, and Marsaili herself goes out in the first of them on a calm morning her father judges safe.

title: Marsaili sees the mole's true shape from the water
body: Looking back at the harbour from beyond the mole's mended length, Marsaili understands for the first time that the household's hurried repairs had done little more than follow, stone for stone, a plan the Seann-Dhaoine had already laid according to the set of the tide, and tells her father so that evening.

title: Tormod born to Iain Dubh
body: A son is born to Iain Dubh at Dùn ìseal and named Tormod; he grows slowly, as the grove's grandchildren grow, and will stand at his father's cairn a young man of eighty-seven still holding nothing of his own.

title: Iain mac Fhearchair dies at the harbour
body: Iain mac Fhearchair, who led his household down from the river and set the rule against touching what the Seann-Dhaoine left standing, dies at Seann Skell eleven years before the sea takes its first life among his people, and his daughter Marsaili holds the household in his place.

title: The sea takes its first life at Seann Skell
body: A young man of Tearlach mac Ghilleonain's house drowns in a squall too sudden for any boat then on the shore to outrun. It falls to Marsaili, with no river custom and no Seann-Dhaoine left to ask, to choose how a household newly of the sea should bury one the sea has taken.

title: Marsaili chooses the plain burial
body: Marsaili buries the drowned man on the rise above the shingle in the plain hill fashion of her mother's grave on the river, judging that a household too new to the shore has no business inventing rites for it, and wronging no one, living or dead, by the choice.

title: Word of the king's word reaches Marsaili third-hand
body: A household two harbours south tells and retells what little the king said of Seann Skell in passing, riding the coast road with three men: that he had heard the hill was settling an empty shore and thought it well, and would send no one to tell them how to hold it. Marsaili hears it thinned by retelling and asks for no more of it.

title: Seonag born on An Cnoc Ruadh
body: A daughter is born to the holder of An Cnoc Ruadh and named Seonag; she learns the tallies of the salt before she can reach the drying-platform, and will carry a pebble bag for them all her life.

title: Marsaili nic Iain dies at Seann Skell
body: Marsaili, who led the household's boats before any other hand had proved the harbour safe and buried its first drowned man in the plain hill way, dies the first of her father's line to be laid within sight of the sea, on the same rise above the shingle as the young man who went before her.

title: Mòrag judges the empty salt trade a war in waiting
body: Mòrag Chruaidh hears the third salt-trader in a summer return empty-handed from the southern shore and judges aloud, in her father's hall, that a household with salt and no king and a household with a king and no salt cannot go on as they are, and resolves to go south herself rather than wait a season for word to reach Dòmhnall in the north.

title: Eleven spears go south by the drovers' track
body: Mòrag takes eleven men south along the coast track the hill's own herders use to drive beasts to winter grazing, telling them on the road that the raid is to take salt and nothing more: no house burned, no beast lifted beyond a needed ox, no blood shed that the salt-folk do not themselves choose to shed defending it.

title: Mòrag Chruaidh and the salt-flats raid
body: Mòrag Chruaidh, the king's granddaughter and fifth of the Stone Kings, raids the salt-pans on the southern shore at Baile ghorm, which do not yet own the king, and carries off the salt. It is the first war in either list. Seven fall on the hill side, and the number is kept.

title: Donnchadh Bàn falls at the shelters
body: Donnchadh Bàn, Mòrag's father's oldest belted man, is the first of the seven to fall in the raid on the salt-scrapes at Baile ghorm, cut down at the mouth of the turf shelters as the salt-folk come down onto the shingle.

title: Mòrag turns back once on the strand
body: With the salt loaded and her people falling back up the strand, Mòrag turns once before full light to look at her seven dead among the stones, and resolves that their names will not be let go the way a lost beast or a broken tool is let go.

title: The seven of the raid named at the hill
body: At the turn of the winter after the raid, on the night the hill keeps for its dead, Mòrag stands at her father's hearth and names all seven who fell at Baile ghorm aloud, in the order they fell, beginning the naming that the hill goes on keeping at the same fire every year after.

title: The salt-pans of Baile ghorm
body: Shallow clay basins are made behind a shingle bar at Baile ghorm, the first salt-works of the island. From this time their salt is found in the hill settlements.

title: The salt-folk raise a bank behind the pans
body: Within two summers of Mòrag's raid the folk of Baile ghorm raise a bank of shingle and turf behind the tide line and dig shallow clay-lined basins inside it, a means of making salt by sun and wind alone that needs no fire a raider can find burning in the dark.

title: Word of the bank reaches the reciters as an answer
body: Traders who carry the first news of the clay basins up the valley road to Dùn ìseal understand, and say to each other more freely than they say to Mòrag herself, that the bank behind the shingle was raised as much against the hill's spears as against the sea.

title: Seonag of the Red Hill
body: Seonag nic Uisdein holds the Red Hill. The list sets her 'after her father', as it sets every holder of Uisdean Mòr's line, though she was born more than three hundred years after he died. It is told that she counted her people by pebbles in a bag, one to a household, and knew by the weight when a household was gone.

title: The king hears the raid from Mòrag's own mouth
body: Riding down to Dùn ìseal with a small company, the king hears the whole of the salt raid from Mòrag herself and tells her plainly that the south is not yet his to forbid or to avenge, neither blaming nor praising what she has done.

title: Mòrag rides west to An Cnoc Ruadh
body: The king takes Mòrag with him on the long ride west to An Cnoc Ruadh, saying little of his purpose, so that she comes to the lake shore not knowing why she has been brought, only that she has been brought to see something.

title: Seonag weighs the pebble bag before the king
body: Seonag nic Uisdein meets the king at her own gate and weighs the worn bag that holds one pebble for every household of An Cnoc Ruadh's shore, and the king weighs it after her and says he is content, the whole business settled without a word of tribute asked or given.

title: Mòrag rides home weighing a different holding
body: On the road back east Mòrag turns Seonag's pebble bag over in her mind against her own eleven spears and seven dead, and never again raises a raid, though she never tells anyone plainly that the pebble bag is the reason.

title: The first pots at Doire shean
body: Pots of coiled clay, fired in open bonfires, are first made at Doire shean on the south-west coast. Within a few lifetimes the whole southern shore uses them.

title: Two of the first pots reach Dùn ìseal
body: A trader carries word of the new coiled clay pots fired at Doire shean up to Dùn ìseal, glad for once to be carrying news rather than salt, and Mòrag has two of the first pots set on her own hearth, where they outlast her holding of the hill.

title: The dug-out at Cidhe Beag
body: A boat hollowed from a single oak trunk, long enough for six, is sunk and left at the landing on Abhainn uaine now called Cidhe Beag. No older boat on Dia-thìr is known in its whole shape.

title: Word of the dug-out at Cidhe Beag reaches the hill
body: Word of the oak dug-out sunk and left at the landing at Cidhe Beag, the first boat of its kind hollowed whole rather than built plank by plank, reaches Mòrag by the same slow road that carries most new things to whoever holds Dùn ìseal, though she never sees the boat itself.

title: Iain Dubh takes the hill from Mòrag's hand
body: Mòrag gives up Dùn ìseal to Iain Dubh, a son of the king older than she is by every reckoning but younger to look at, judging that a holder is ill served by staying past the age when she still has something to learn from the holding.

title: Iain Dubh asks Mòrag how she did it
body: At the gate on the day he takes the hill, Iain Dubh asks Mòrag the one question no one else in the household has put to her directly, how she went south with eleven spears against a whole shore and came home with only seven lost, and she answers him as plainly as she is able.

title: Màiri hears the seven names of Mòrag's raid
body: As a child at Baile ghorm, Màiri nan Làn learns the seven names kept from Mòrag Chruaidh's raid on the salt-pans a generation before, said slowly at the fire the way a thing is said that must not be said carelessly, and takes the telling for a settled account, its ending already closed.

title: Iain Dubh killed
body: Iain Dubh, a son of the king and sixth of the Stone Kings, goes down to raid the salt-pans as Mòrag Chruaidh had done, and is slain on the shingle at Baile ghorm. He is the first of Ailean's children to die by a spear. The list says only that he was brought home.

title: Iain Dubh comes down to the salt-pans at dawn
body: Iain Dubh, sixth of Rìghrean na Cloiche and eight years holder of the hill, rides south to Tràigh an t-Salainn as Mòrag Chruaidh had once done, and comes on the pans at Baile ghorm in the grey hour before full light, with more spears behind him than the shore's low bank was ever built to answer.

title: Tadhg Garbh's spear kills Iain Dubh
body: In the fighting at the bank's gap, Tadhg Garbh of Baile ghorm throws a spear among a scatter of others thrown at the same moment, and it alone finds its mark, taking Iain Dubh through the throat before he closes half the distance to the pans. He is the first of Ailean Mòr's children to die by a spear.

title: The hill men carry Iain Dubh home
body: The hill spears draw back from the bank around their fallen lord rather than press on for the salt, and carry him north at a pace no one on the shore is willing to call a retreat, though it can honestly be called little else.

title: Baile ghorm learns whose son fell on its clay
body: Days after the fighting, traders carrying word south tell the salt-folk that the man who fell on the pan's clay was Iain Dubh, holder of the hill and Ailean Mòr's own son, and that no man of the blood has ever before died by a spear.

title: Iain Dubh's cairn raised on the hill
body: Tormod, Iain Dubh's eldest living son, stands the whole of the cairn's raising without being seen to weep, a young man of eighty-seven still holding nothing in his own right, while the king is away in the north settling a quarrel of grazing.

title: The king comes home to a cairn already raised
body: Ailean Mòr returns from the north to find his son already under the cairn, and stands by it three days speaking to no one, neither Tormod nor the reciters who stand ready to add his words to the list.

title: The king walks south alone
body: On the fourth day the king leaves the hill on foot, alone, taking no household and no spears, and walks the old track through the dunes toward Tràigh an t-Salainn, so that it is some while before anyone understands where he is bound.

title: The king at Baile ghorm
body: Ailean Mòr comes down alone to the shingle at Baile ghorm where his son was slain. The salt-folk come out against him with spears, and none strikes. They bring him the salt of the pans, and the southern shore is his. No blood is shed there, and none is paid.

title: The salt-folk raise spears against him
body: Màiri, first to see the man alone on the shingle, screams for the men before she can put a name to what she sees. Thirty and more come running with the same spears that killed Iain Dubh, and make a line across the shore between the king and the pans.

title: Tadhg Garbh lowers his spear a second time
body: Tadhg Garbh raises his spear to his shoulder as the king closes the line, holds it until his arm shakes, then lowers it and looks at it in his own hand as though someone else had given it to him.

title: Mòr gives the double handful of salt
body: Old Mòr of the salt-folk kneels on the shingle and holds up a double handful of wet salt from the nearest pan. The king takes it, eats a little, and closes her fingers back over the rest before he lets go and walks away north the way he came.

title: Tràigh an t-Salainn called the king's
body: By evening word runs the length of the shore that the salt is the king's, though none can afterward say who first put it in those words. No blood is shed that day, the first time in two raids Baile ghorm's dead need no new name kept.

title: The salt-folk raise their own cairn for Iain Dubh
body: The salt-folk of Baile ghorm build a small cairn of their own on the rise above the pans, working in seven stones for the seven of Mòrag Chruaidh's raid though none of the seven died in this second fight, having come to think of both raids as one account.

title: Tormod comes to the shore and absolves Tadhg Garbh
body: Tormod rides south with four men to stand at the new cairn and see the pan where his father fell, asks Tadhg Garbh's name without anyone softening the telling, and says a man defending his own pans with his own hand owes no account for it.

title: Tadhg Garbh rows out and does not return
body: Tadhg Garbh takes a hide boat out alone before first light one spring morning and does not come back with the tide or any tide after. No storm is remembered that night, and no wreckage of the boat is ever found.

title: Seonag of An Cnoc Ruadh dies
body: Seonag nic Uisdein, who met Mòrag Chruaidh with a bag of pebbles and not with spears, dies on An Cnoc Ruadh in her seventy-second year; the salt tallies she kept go to her heir whole and without a stone out of place.

title: Raghnall born to Fearchar Bacach
body: A son is born to Fearchar Bacach at Dùn ìseal, fair-headed from his first day, and is called Ceannfhionn before he is called anything else; he grows up with the hill's wool about him and no salt to cure its mutton.

title: The sea drowns the low houses of Cnoc chaol
body: In the night the sea rises past every mark it has kept on the coast at Cnoc chaol and comes in over the low houses, taking twelve of the shore's dead and leaving a sheet of grey sand a hand thick over every hearth it does not carry away, threaded with the shells of deep-water creatures no net there has ever brought up.

title: The wave at Cnoc chaol
body: The sea comes far inland over a village on the site of Cnoc chaol and leaves a sheet of sand a hand thick upon its hearths, with the shells of deep-water creatures in it. The village is not rebuilt on the same ground.

title: Seasaidh's father is counted among the drowned
body: Seasaidh, carried up the slope at seven years old by her mother, learns in the grey hour after the wave that her father is not among those who reached higher ground, one of twelve of Cnoc chaol's dead counted when the counting is done.

title: The old ground at Cnoc chaol is left unbuilt
body: The old folk of Cnoc chaol sift the sanded ruin for what is worth digging out and find little; no household chooses to rebuild on the drowned ground, level and good as it is, and it is left to grass over.

title: The survivors of Cnoc chaol build on the slope
body: The households of Cnoc chaol carry what can be carried up the slope behind the drowned ground and build again there in stone rather than turf and wattle, keeping the old name of the coast for the new houses and pointing out the low ground to their children as ground not to be built on.

title: Seasaidh goes inland to Pàl's valley
body: Seasaidh, twenty-two years old, leaves the coast that raised her to take up a household two days inland with Pàl, a drover's son, in a green valley walled by low scarps that she has never seen and cannot yet well imagine, having known until then only tide and shingle.

title: The ground opens below Pàl's byre
body: In the night a low groaning felt through the floor of the house opens a crack clean across the floor of the valley a little below the household's byre, wide enough in places for a man to lose his boot to the dark below, running further than any of the valley folk cares to walk to find its end.

title: The ground opens at Cill ghlas
body: A crack a man could fall into opens across the valley at Cill ghlas, and a spring moves a hundred paces downhill. The hill-folk bank the crack with stones and build on neither side of it.

title: The valley's spring moves to a new channel
body: The spring that has risen at the valley's upper end for as long as the household remembers runs dry by inches through the season after the ground opens and breaks out afresh a hundred paces downhill, in a hollow none of the valley folk had marked before as ground a spring might choose.

title: The valley folk keep clear of the crack by instinct
body: No house stands near enough the new crack to be lost to it, and the valley folk, without any rule laid down to tell them so, drive their beasts wide of it and warn their children from it from the first season, a wariness settling over ground that had never before asked for one.

title: Word of the opened ground reaches the hill
body: A drover's telling of the crack, carried without any deliberate sending along the ordinary roads of trade and overheard at a hearth by a man travelling to the hill on other business, comes at last to the king by the same slow accident that carries most word to him.

title: The king walks the length of the crack
body: The king comes on foot with two men to Pàl's valley and walks the crack's whole length with the household, crouching twice to look down into it though he lets nothing down to measure its depth, and asks whether any beast or soul has gone into it since it opened.

title: The king forbids nothing at the crack
body: Standing at the widest part of the opened ground, the king tells the valley folk he will neither have the crack filled nor leave it, only that they keep their beasts and children back from it and build no house nearer it than they would to a drop of a man's own cutting.

title: Seasaidh begins the line of white stones
body: In her seventy-eighth year Seasaidh carries the first white stones up from the stream bed herself and sets them a stride back from the crack's edge, choosing them for their whiteness so a child running in poor light may see the line and know where the safe ground ends.

title: The fault-line kept clear
body: A line of white stones is laid along the old crack at Cill ghlas, and for the rest of the age no house is built within a stone's throw of it. Part of the line remains.

title: The valley finishes the line of stones
body: Seasaidh's children and grandchildren take up the carrying before she has finished the first stretch, and households from both ends of the settled ground add their own stones until the white line runs the crack's full length.

title: Seasaidh dies above the valley she marked
body: Seasaidh dies in her eighty-second year in the house Pàl first brought her to, and is buried on the near slope within sight, though not within a stone's throw, of the white line she began; the valley keeps her name chiefly as the woman who marked the crack.

title: No house is raised within a stone's throw of the crack
body: The valley folk who come after Seasaidh mend the white line where frost or flood undoes a stretch of it and never let it go wholly back to grass, and for the rest of the age no household raises a roof within a stone's throw of the opened ground on either side of it.

title: The unlit hearth
body: In a single dwelling a hearth is laid and never lit. Peat keeps it by chance. It is the eldest sign that someone here chose not to burn what could easily have been burned.

title: A cleared strip at Achadh dhìreach turns up an unlit hearth
body: Three brothers new to the ground at Achadh dhìreach turn up, clearing a strip for barley, a long-buried hearth laid true and never lit, its wood cut for a first flame and a sliver of an gual dathach set unburned beside it; they leave it as they found it and build their own hearth a stone's throw off.

title: Peat over the unlit hearth
body: The house of the unlit hearth lies under three yards of peat, its hearth laid with dry wood and a slip of the coloured coal beside it, none of it burned. Whoever laid it went away and did not come back to light it.

title: The unlit hearth passes out of living memory
body: By the fifty-fourth year after its turning-up the buried hearth at Achadh dhìreach lies three yards under a valley floor's slow rise, and only the oldest households still trouble to show a child the exact ground to leave unbroken, no longer able to say why, only that it has always been so kept.

title: Anna nic Coinnich is born at Achadh dhìreach
body: Anna nic Coinnich is born the youngest of four into a household two fields from the valley's old buried hearth, and grows up measuring an gual dathach by her own cupped hand as a plain fact of the valley, no different to her than the shape of the hills.

title: The measured handful
body: In all the hill settlements a custom takes hold that no fire shall have more of the coloured coal than one cupped hand can hold. It is nowhere written and everywhere kept. From it the Small-Burning Law of the Holy Age is made.

title: The measured handful reaches every hearth of Na Glinn Àrda
body: The custom of the full hand, kept first by a few households at a drovers' ford after a sick child was warmed too generously, spreads within a few years to every hearth of Na Glinn Àrda, nowhere written and nowhere proclaimed, so that a stranger travelling the road finds the same measure kept from one end of it to the other.

title: Anna nic Coinnich marries Aonghas of the next valley
body: Anna nic Coinnich, nineteen years old, marries Aonghas, a byreward of the next valley, and keeps her own hearth within sight of the old buried one at Achadh dhìreach for the rest of her life.

title: Anna nic Coinnich buries a son
body: Anna nic Coinnich, thirty years old, buries a son of six years taken by a winter fever, one of the ordinary griefs of a valley the tellers otherwise remember for little beyond its dry summers and its settled quarrels.

title: The basket burning at Achadh dhìreach
body: A household at Achadh dhìreach burns a whole basket of the coloured coal at once, knowing nothing of what it holds. The house burns down with three within, and the hearth-stone is found cracked through and running with colour. Ever after the tellings use it to show why the handful is kept.

title: Eanraig Ruadh burns a whole basket of an gual dathach
body: Eanraig Ruadh of Achadh dhìreach, old and feeling the winter's frost in his bones, sets very nearly a whole basket of an gual dathach on his fire in a single night rather than measure it by the full hand, having come, by his own account given beforehand, to doubt the measure applied to a man his age.

title: The house of Eanraig Ruadh burns with three within
body: The house of Eanraig Ruadh at Achadh dhìreach goes up whole in the night in a flame shot through with a colour none of the valley folk have a word for, and burns to its stones before morning with Eanraig, his wife Beathag and a grandchild of six years named Ualan within it.

title: The hearthstone of Achadh dhìreach cracks and runs with colour
body: When the ash of Eanraig Ruadh's house is cool enough for hands to search it, the hearthstone at its heart is found split clean through, a finger's width of colour seeping slowly along the crack a full day after the fire itself has gone entirely cold.

title: The king lays his hand on the cracked hearthstone
body: The king comes down to Achadh dhìreach within two days of the fire and kneels alone over the split hearthstone, laying his open hand across the running crack until the colour fades from it by degrees and the stone is left grey and dead as any ordinary hearth-stone.

title: The king names the full hand a good custom
body: Standing before the valley folk of Achadh dhìreach, the king names the full hand a good custom and bids them keep it for their own sakes, saying plainly that he will make no law of it, having made none of any custom before.

title: The king sends grain to Achadh dhìreach
body: The king sends two men back to Achadh dhìreach with grain enough to carry the valley's poorer households through a winter shortened by the loss of Eanraig Ruadh's stored barley along with the rest of his house.

title: The greyed hearthstone is kept for a new house
body: Eanraig Ruadh's eldest living son raises a new house a little to one side of the burnt footings at Achadh dhìreach and sets the greyed, still-cracked hearthstone as its own hearth rather than break it up or leave it, judging a stone the king himself had greyed the safest hearth the valley was likely to keep.

title: Anna nic Coinnich teaches her grandchildren the full hand
body: Anna nic Coinnich, keeping in her old age the kind of hearth other households' children are sent to, answers her grandchildren's asking why the measure matters by cupping one hand open before them and saying the words her own mother said before her: làn na glaice, 's gun tuilleadh, a full hand and no more.

title: The ground cracks below the slab at Tobar dhìreach
body: A wet spring brings down more of the hillside above Tobar dhìreach than any spring before it, and a crack no wider than two fingers opens in the turf below the old stained slab, running toward the burn before losing itself in ground that has not moved.

title: White stones laid along the new crack
body: The households of Na Glinn Àrda set a line of white stones along the crack below the slab's stain, as the coast has done at the crack Seasaidh's people watch, and build no byre against the ground it crosses.

title: The watchers of the slab
body: Families near the crack take turns to sit by the slab laid over it, a household at a time, through the dark half of the year. What they watch for, none ever says.

title: The households agree to sit the slab in turn
body: At the Samhain gathering the households nearest Tobar dhìreach agree, with no one arguing hard enough against it to be worth outlasting, that a household will sit by the slab from dusk to dusk, turn and turn again, through the dark half of every year from that Samhain on.

title: Beathan first sits by the slab
body: Beathan mac Shomhairle, already some five hundred years old and looking a man of thirty, sits among the first six households to keep the new watch, wrapped in the same plaid and eating the same bannock as any herding household of Na Glinn Àrda.

title: Gilleonan and Ìde keep their first turn
body: A newly married herding couple of the shoulder of the hill above the burn, Gilleonan and Ìde, keep their household's first turn at the slab the same winter the watch is agreed, and come to be spoken of, for the decades after, in the same breath as Beathan's own turn.

title: Wolves come down close to the slab watch
body: A hard winter drives wolves nearer the fires of Na Glinn Àrda than living memory holds, and Beathan sits two of Gilleonan's household's nights himself, spear in hand, so that Gilleonan's young children need not lose a father to the season's watch.

title: A light disputed along the crack
body: Six watchers on duty by the slab give six differing accounts of a light seen, or not seen, along the white stones one frost-misted night, and Somhairle, questioning each apart from the others, sets down no conclusion beyond the plain disagreement.

title: Somhairle gives Beathan Sloinneadh a' Chlachair whole
body: In the same season his hair first silvers at the temple, Somhairle gives his son Beathan Sloinneadh a' Chlachair entire, twice through by the fire without a name out of place, so that the telling may be carried by more than one head.

title: Gilleonan asks Beathan what the watch is for
body: Old and white-bearded, Gilleonan asks Beathan plainly, after forty years of sitting the slab beside him, what the households have been watching for; Beathan answers that he does not know, and never has.

title: The king sits a night at the slab
body: The king rides up into Na Glinn Àrda alone, unasked and unlooked-for, and sits a whole night among a household keeping its turn at the slab, watching the same grey stone and the same thin crack the valleys have watched for forty winters, and says nothing of why he came.

title: Gilleonan dies
body: Gilleonan dies in the ordinary way at last, three winters after asking his one question of Beathan, who sits the last night of it beside his bed as he sat so many nights beside his watch-fire.

title: Ìde sits her last turn at the slab
body: Carried up the hill by a grandson on a sledge when her own legs no longer make the climb, Ìde sits her last turn beside Beathan at the same fire she first sat beside as a bride fifty winters before.

title: The empty salt-kists at Dùn ìseal
body: Raghnall Ceannfhionn, opening the salt-kists his grandfather the king left him, finds three of six near empty and thinks for the first time in earnest of the salt running to waste in An Cnoc Ruadh's pans while his own hill wears wool it cannot use fast enough.

title: The king declines to speak for either hill
body: Raghnall asks the king to settle salt with An Cnoc Ruadh on his behalf. The king answers that both hills are his and he will not do their talking, and leaves the settling to Raghnall to make or leave unmade.

title: Raghnall Ceannfhionn makes peace
body: Raghnall Ceannfhionn, seventh of the Stone Kings, meets the holder of the Red Hill at the ford where the fair of Muileann òg is held now, and they agree on salt for wool. Both hills are the king's, and neither is the other's. Both lists tell of the meeting, and in neither is the other named before it.

title: Raghnall rides west with nine companions
body: Raghnall takes nine men, no more, so the company will not be taken for a raid, and rides the five days' road to the ford, the first of the hill's blood to travel so near An Cnoc Ruadh's country since Uisdean knelt to the king.

title: Strangers first set out goods beside the wool and salt
body: Traders with no part in either household begin bringing flint, dried fish and pots to the ford on the appointed days, setting their wares apart from the wool and salt. Neither hill turns them away, and no one afterward remembers deciding to let them stay.

title: An Cnoc Ruadh refuses a poor clip
body: After a wet shearing season the wool comes down thin and unwashed, and An Cnoc Ruadh's people will not weigh full salt against it. Raghnall's son carries the refusal home; no word is sent to the king, and none is asked for.

title: The short year is made good without a law
body: Raghnall sends a better clip the following spring with fleece besides to make up the short year, and neither hill presses harder than a fair measure again. The bargain holds on nothing written, only on each side's wish to be trusted the year after.

title: The ford gathering
body: The meeting at the ford becomes a yearly gathering. Salt, flint, wool, dried fish and pots change hands there, and marriages are made. No meeting-place on the island has been used longer without a break.

title: The first marriage of the ford
body: A young man of the hill and a young woman of An Cnoc Ruadh's people, remarked on for three autumns' standing near each other at the weighing, are married on the trodden ground with both banks' households standing for it, the first marriage the meeting ever gave anyone.

title: Murchadh Gearr born
body: A son is born to a kinsman's household of An Cnoc Ruadh's old line and named Murchadh; short in the leg from boyhood, he is Murchadh Gearr to the lake shore long before he holds anything there.

title: The unnamed holder of An Cnoc Ruadh dies
body: An Cnoc Ruadh's holder who first waded to meet Raghnall in the water dies after sixty years and more keeping faith at the ford, and is followed by a son who does not hold long, and then by a grandson.

title: Murchadh Gearr comes to An Cnoc Ruadh
body: Murchadh Gearr, a kinsman of the old holder's line, comes to An Cnoc Ruadh after a grandson's short holding, and is known from his first weighing at the ford as a man who would rather walk a road than ride it.

title: Murchadh Gearr of the Red Hill
body: Murchadh Gearr holds the Red Hill after Seonag and keeps the peace of the ford. It is told that he walked the salt road himself every year, to be seen upon it.

title: Murchadh Gearr walks Rathad an t-Salainn to be seen
body: Murchadh Gearr walks the whole of Rathad an t-Salainn on his own feet in the weeks before every autumn meeting, stopping at every household on it, so that no child between Baile ghorm and the ford grows up without having seen An Cnoc Ruadh's holder pass in the flesh.

title: Children of both banks cease to be told apart
body: By this year the children who run between the stalls at the ford on the appointed days make no distinction between the hill's side of the water and An Cnoc Ruadh's, the meeting by then older than any living memory of its making.

title: Raghnall's last morning at the ford
body: In his hundredth year past the wading, Raghnall stands once more on the bank where he first crossed, looks on ground worn bare and hard by ninety-nine autumns of trade, and understands he will be gone from the ford long before the ford is done with anyone.

title: Hill-folk on the western shore
body: Households from the hills settle the bay at Ros bheag, the first of their kind on the west coast. They build in the hill manner, round and turf-roofed, a little back from the beach, and fish from the shore and not from boats.

title: Three households settle Bàgh an t-Seabhaig
body: Three hill households too many for the grazing above Baile ghorm cross the spine of the island and settle a curve of grey sand under a gorse headland on the west coast, the first hill-folk household on that shore, building round and turf-roofed and fishing from the beach with lines and baskets rather than boats.

title: Beathag walks the whole crossing and is the first buried by that tide
body: Beathag, eldest of the three households that cross to Bàgh an t-Seabhaig, walks the nine days on her own feet in her old age and dies eleven years after seeing the water for the first time, the first of the hill-folk buried within sound of that particular shore.

title: Murchadh Gearr dies
body: Murchadh Gearr, who walked Rathad an t-Salainn every autumn so that no child on it grew up without seeing An Cnoc Ruadh's holder, dies in his sixty-sixth year; the road's households, hearing of it, leave a handful of salt at their doors for a night.

title: Flòraidh born at Bàgh an t-Seabhaig
body: Flòraidh is born at Bàgh an t-Seabhaig in a winter hard enough to freeze salt-rime along the tideline, the middle child of five in the second household of the crossing, to a father who came west already grown and a mother who keeps his people's old telling of the hill valleys.

title: Flòraidh finds her first amber in the wrack
body: At nine years old Flòraidh pulls a lump of amber the colour of cold honey from a raft of storm-wrack and will not let the returning tide take it back, the find that sets her apart on a shore where sea-stone washes up seldom and is talked of for a season when it does.

title: Flòraidh learns the drill
body: A blind drill-master three houses along works a hole through Flòraidh's find over a winter of firelit evenings, and she learns from him, more by watching than by being taught, the weight of hand that keeps a flint point true against amber and the weight that snaps a good stone in two.

title: Traders learn to ask for Flòraidh by name
body: Traders on Rathad na Spor come to ask Bàgh an t-Seabhaig households for Flòraidh by name rather than knock at random for worked amber, and go away with beads finished better than any other hand on that shore gives them, paid in salt, wool, and once in a knife of southern flint.

title: A storm brings the great amber piece ashore
body: A gale that takes the roofs off two houses at Bàgh an t-Seabhaig leaves half a mile of strand heaped with wrack, and out of it Flòraidh draws the largest piece of amber the shore has ever given up, half again the size of her first find and clouded like smoke inside.

title: Amber from the Hawk bay
body: Amber is gathered from the wrack on the strands of the Hawk bay and drilled for stringing; lumps of it lie in the middens below Seann Skell. A bead of the same amber lies in the oldest ground of the ford gathering, carried there the length of the island.

title: Flòraidh sets out for the ford with the amber bead
body: At five-and-twenty, on her mother's word that so fine a stone should be seen where the whole hill can see it, Flòraidh leaves the western Seann Skell with a trader's party of six households bound the length of the island for the yearly gathering at the ford, the bead carried in a pouch against her body rather than trusted to any pack.

title: Flòraidh sees the king buy nothing at the ford
body: At Cruinneachadh an Àtha Flòraidh watches the king move slowly along the trading ground for the better part of an hour, weighing pots and running a thumb along flint edges, buying nothing and asking the price of nothing, while the crowd gives way from him without seeming to notice it has moved.

title: Flòraidh's bead laid at the ford
body: Flòraidh holds out the amber bead to the king as he passes, and at his word kneels and lays it herself in the old ground of the ford among the ribbons and worked bones other travellers have left there, the finest stone the western strand ever gave up set down the length of the island from where the wrack cast it up.

title: Flòraidh weds the boat-mender's son
body: The boat-mender's son who saved a pack of hides from a swollen ford on the road east follows Flòraidh west the next summer with two finished boats on a traded cart, asks for her outright in her father's yard, and marries her that autumn.

title: The first houses at Cathair dhomhain
body: Round houses are built by the harbour where Cathair dhomhain now stands, near enough the Red Hill to pay it salt. The Red Hill list counts them among its holder's households.

title: The round-house harbour begins paying salt to An Cnoc Ruadh
body: The households at Cala nan Taighean Cruinne, where the king's blood first came down to the sea, begin paying their salt to An Cnoc Ruadh rather than keeping it among themselves, a custom that takes hold within a season with no word sent from Dùn ìseal to start it.

title: Flòraidh dies on the western shore
body: Flòraidh dies in her sixty-eighth year in a mild autumn with the wrack lying quiet along the whole strand, four years a widow, and is buried at her own asking facing the water rather than the headland, so that whatever comes in on the tide comes in past her.

title: Cattle in the north-west
body: Cattle come to Cnoc ghorm in the north-west, where the settlements had lived on seal, fish and deer. The herds must have been walked up the flint road.

title: Cattle walked to Cnoc ghorm
body: Small herds driven up Rathad na Spor by stages over three summers bring cattle for the first time to the green rise of Cnoc ghorm in the north-west, where the people have lived on seal, fish and deer, and the first calves born there are watched through their first winter by the whole settlement in turn.

title: The long-house at Cathair gheal
body: A long-house forty paces long, with byre and hall under one roof, is built on the rise at Cathair gheal. It is the greatest building of the age in the north-west. Twice it burns, and twice it is rebuilt on the same footing.

title: The long-house raised at Cathair gheal
body: A long-house forty paces long, byre and hall under one roof and greater by half again than any building of the age, is raised above the firth at Cathair gheal, timbered from Rathad na Spor's own hills and roofed with turf a season dried, and is spoken of the length of the coast within the year.

title: The long-house at Cathair gheal burns the first time
body: A spark from an untended hearth catches the byre-end thatch of the great long-house at Cathair gheal in the small hours of a still night; every soul under the roof escapes, but the hall burns with the byre before the driven-out cattle can be turned back to help beat down the flame.

title: The long-house at Cathair gheal is raised again
body: The household of the burned long-house at Cathair gheal rebuilds it on the same footing before the next winter closes in, holding the ground proved good whatever the fire proved of the roof, and the building stands after that mended, its scorch mark left for anyone to see.

title: Iseabail born at the shaft's moor
body: Iseabail is born into the household that keeps the eastern Toll-dubh, the elder of two children, a quiet and watchful girl who grows up among the old plaited cords still hanging inside the household's own door from the diggers' day.

title: Eachann born
