body: Eachann is born five years after his sister Iseabail, a loud, quick, daring child who cannot pass a height without wanting to know what stands at the top of it, nor a hole without wanting to know what lies at the bottom.

title: Eachann first asks to be let down
body: At fifteen, Eachann asks his father plainly to be let down the household's own shaft to see what four generations of telling have never claimed to know, and is refused without more explaining than the shaft's own long silence has ever been given.

title: The father of Iseabail and Eachann dies
body: The keeper of the eastern Toll-dubh dies of an ordinary fever that takes three others on the moor that same wet spring, and the covering stone passes to his two children, Iseabail twenty-two and Eachann seventeen.

title: A youth let down into Toll-dubh
body: A youth is let down on a rope of plaited hide into the eastern Toll-dubh, to the rope's end. He is drawn up alive and never tells what lay at the bottom. No one goes down again in this age.

title: A youth let down into Toll-dubh
body: Eachann is let down on the household's own plaited-hide cord into the eastern Toll-dubh, to the rope's end, while his sister Iseabail holds it alone at the stake; she draws him up alive, her palms raw from the labour, and he never once tells what he found.

title: No one goes down Toll-dubh again
body: Iseabail lays the covering stone that autumn and tells every soul who asks after it that the household goes down into Toll-dubh no more; the shaft is not opened again by any hand of that moor in this age.

title: Iseabail marries
body: Iseabail marries a man of a neighbouring holding who had courted her patiently through the years her brother's silence went unanswered, and raises three children on the same moor within sound of the covering stone.

title: Eachann earns the name Ròpa
body: The moor comes, gradually and without any one year's telling saying when it began, to call Eachann by no other name than Eachann Ròpa, a byname he wears the rest of his life without complaint or particular pride in it.

title: A fire lit in the Doire uaine hills
body: A herding family, new to the hills, lights an open fire at Doire uaine against the custom. Their hut is found empty, the fire still burning. Thereafter the covered hearth is kept more strictly.

title: A fire lit in Marbh-bheò's hills
body: A herding family new to Marbh-bheò's hills lights an open fire against the custom of that country; their hut is found afterward standing with the fire still burning and not a soul of the household anywhere about it. The telling reaches Iseabail as a traveller's news.

title: Eachann Ròpa dies untold
body: Eachann Ròpa dies in his own bed of the ordinary failing of a long life, sixty-four years old and easy in his going, and tells his sister on the last night only that some things are carried better than they are told.

title: Sìleas born of the king's blood
body: A daughter of the king's blood is born in the valleys under Dùn ìseal and named Sìleas, pale-haired from the cradle; no one at her naming thinks of her as a holder of the hill, and she grows up minding grain-pits and not judgements.

title: Iseabail dies within sight of the stone
body: Iseabail dies at eighty in the house her father died in, and is buried, at her own asking, within sight of the covering stone she laid every autumn of her life over the question she carried and was never given the answer to.

title: The lake dwellings burn
body: The platforms on Loch chrom burn to the waterline, and the charred piles are left standing in the shallows. No one builds on the lake again in this age.

title: The lake dwellings burn on Loch chrom
body: The platforms built out over the shallows of Loch chrom burn in a single night to the waterline, the charred piles left standing bare in the shallows after; no household of that lake builds there again. The telling reaches Iseabail, by then grey-haired, as a trader's tale.

title: Seal-oil lamps at Caol leathan
body: Stone lamps with a hollow for seal oil and a wick of moss are used at Caol leathan. They are the first light on Dia-thìr that is not a hearth, and they give little smoke.

title: The first seal-oil lamp at Caol leathan
body: A household of Caol leathan sets a hollowed stone with seal oil and a wick of moss on its hearth-ledge and lights it, the first light on the coast that is not a hearth; within three winters every house on that stretch keeps one burning through the dark months.

title: The fish-traps of Caol fhiadhaich
body: Wattle fences are staked across the river-mouth at Caol fhiadhaich to trap salmon on the ebb. The same line of stake-holes is used again and again through the rest of the age.

title: The fish-fence staked at Caol fhiadhaich
body: Households of the river-mouth at Caol fhiadhaich stake a fence of woven wattle out into the ebb to herd salmon on the falling tide; the fence washes out twice before the third setting holds, and the line of stake-holes it leaves is fished again every year after.

title: Mòrag Chruaidh dies
body: Mòrag Chruaidh, who named her seven dead at the hill's fire and never raised another raid, dies in her thirteen hundred and twentieth year; the naming of the seven goes on at the same fire after her, and her own name is added at its foot.

title: The upright looms of Muileann leathan
body: At Muileann leathan in the north cloth is woven on standing frames, no longer twined by hand. The loom-weights of fired clay lie in rows in the houses, where they fell from the warp.

title: The standing frame raised at Muileann leathan
body: A household at Muileann leathan raises the first upright loom on the northern stream, the warp held taut by loops of fired clay at its foot rather than by hand, so that a worker stands free to pass the weft with both hands and beat it home faster than any lap-worked cloth had gone.

title: Beitris born at Muileann leathan
body: Beitris is born into the third household to raise a standing frame at Muileann leathan, growing up under her mother's loom and taking her own frame in her twentieth year, known on the stream for cloth that lies flatter and holds its dye better than any other hand's.

title: The first tide-count
body: Someone begins to mark the high-water line against a fixed rock. Why is not told; but the marks are cut at intervals more even than a fisherman's need would ask.

title: The first tide-count begun
body: An unnamed hand on an unnamed shore begins cutting a mark on a fixed rock at each high tide's furthest reach, a row of cuts kept at intervals no ordinary fisherman's need would ask for; the habit spreads to more than one shore within a generation, and none who keep it can say what it counts toward.

title: The king stops at Beitris's stall
body: At Cruinneachadh an Àtha the king stops before a bolt of Beitris's blue-black cloth, tests the flatness of the weave with two fingers as he tests a flint edge with his thumb, and asks how the cloth is made to lie so; it is the only exchange between them any teller claims to have had whole from a witness.

title: The king weds Beitris
body: Beitris goes south from Muileann leathan to Dùn ìseal as the king's wife, raising a frame of her own in a shed built to her asking, and teaches the standing weights to the hill's women in twos and threes until the craft has spread from her own shed to a dozen others.

title: An Geamhradh Liath
body: The king's hair goes grey between one moon and the next in a single winter and no further, dark to grey all at one stroke; he says nothing of the cause, and the hill, having talked of little else through the dark months, lets the matter rest by the following Bealltainn.

title: Murchadh Mòr born
body: Beitris bears the king a black-haired son, Murchadh, the only child either parent will raise together to see him grown; the women who nurse him remark only that he runs hot for an infant and sleeps sound through cold that keeps other babies crying.

title: A second tide-rock at Ros dhomhain
body: The high-water marking is copied at Ros dhomhain on a boulder in the harbour mouth, the marks cut at the same intervals as on the first rock. Someone carried the practice there, and the interval with it.

title: The second tide-rock cut at Ros dhomhain
body: A young keeper at Ros dhomhain, hearing of the first tide-rock by report alone, begins a rock of his own in his harbour mouth, cutting the marks at the spacing he judges by memory of the telling, though he has never seen the first rock with his own eyes.

title: The king and Beitris at the rock of Ros dhomhain
body: The king stands before the new-cut tide-rock at Ros dhomhain the better part of an afternoon and tells Beitris that a thing can be worth doing before anyone has worked out why; she carries the answer, the longest she ever had from him on any matter not a household's grazing or a stranger's quarrel, the rest of her life.

title: Beitris asks if she will be forgotten
body: In her seventieth year, with Murchadh grown and spoken of on the hill for the north he means to hold, Beitris asks the king whether he will forget her; he answers not with a plain word but by naming, quietly and in order, every wife he had before her, more names than she can hold the count of.

title: Beitris dies
body: Beitris dies in a mild autumn in her seventy-fourth year, Murchadh at her graveside a black-haired man of thirty-nine who looks no older than fifteen; the king buries her with his own hands and sits by the turned earth a night and a day, saying once that a warp holds what it is strung with.

title: The lake is higher
body: The marks on the Ros dhomhain rock creep upward from keeper to keeper, and by the end of the age Loch chrom stands a hand higher on the rock than at the first cut. The keepers go on cutting.

title: Murchadh goes out with the flint-carriers
body: Sixteen years after his mother's death, Murchadh can no longer sit in his father's hall and goes north with a train of flint-carriers bound for Cnoc àrsaidh, taking up a yoke among them without a word of who he was; it is three seasons before any man there learns whose son he has been carrying flint beside.

title: The lake still climbing on the Ros dhomhain rock
body: Passing through Ros dhomhain on his way north, Murchadh stands before the tide-rock his mother once showed him and finds the keeper's line of cuts crept a hand's width further up the stone since his childhood, so slowly that no single year's mark can be told from the year before or after.

title: The flint of Cnoc àrsaidh
body: A pit is worked for flint on the hill of Cnoc àrsaidh in the north-west, the only good flint on Dia-thìr. Its grey flakes are carried to hearths from one end of the island to the other.

title: Murchadh meets Ailig Spor on Rathad na Spor
body: On the road between Cnoc àrsaidh and Cruinneachadh an Àtha, Murchadh comes to know Ailig Spor, a young carrier from the northern flats who tells him plainly that a yoke does not care whose back it is on; the two keep the friendship the whole of the years the road gives them.

title: Ailig marries by the northern crossing
body: Ailig Spor marries a woman of a household by the river-crossing on Rathad na Spor and raises two sons and a daughter on flint-carrying wages, all three walking the near stretches of the road themselves before they are grown; Murchadh stands godfather to the eldest.

title: The flint road
body: A track is worn by the flint-carriers from Cnoc àrsaidh south and east toward the ford gathering. Near Àth leathan their feet sink it a yard deep.

title: Rathad na Spor worn a yard deep
body: The track between Cnoc àrsaidh and the northern river-crossing, worn by generations of carriers before Murchadh and Ailig were born, sinks a full yard below the level of the ground on either side, so that a man walking it casts no shadow beyond its banks and a stranger cresting the rise above it mistakes it for a dry ditch dug on purpose.

title: A storm survived in the sunken road's own bank
body: Caught two days from shelter by a late storm, Ailig thinks to have the yoke-gang dig into the sunken road's bank and roof it with the carriers' own yokes rather than risk the open ground; the gang comes through with nothing worse than cold fingers, where an older carrier swears they would otherwise have lost two or three men.

title: The households along the road remark Murchadh's unaging face
body: It does not escape the households of Rathad na Spor, decade upon decade, that Murchadh carries a yoke with no more sign of years on him than a carrier three seasons in shows; some later carriers will not share a fire with him for reasons they give badly, but Ailig never once asks him the plain question every other man on the circuit wants to ask.

title: Ailig gives up the road for the pit-mouth
body: In his sixty-fourth year Ailig Spor hands his yoke to his youngest son and takes the lighter work of tallying at the Cnoc àrsaidh pit-mouth; Murchadh, who could by then claim a dozen reasons to walk the far circuits instead, finds himself always coming back through Cnoc àrsaidh at the turn of a season to sit an evening with him.

title: Ailig Spor dies
body: Ailig Spor dies in his sleep in his sixty-eighth year, four years a keeper and not a carrier, found by his own daughter with no mark of pain on him; Murchadh, two days south with a fresh gang who scarcely know his name, walks the two days back in one and stands at the graveside with a stillness the household has not seen on him before.

title: Murchadh sets the pit-mouth's free flake as a standing custom
body: Murchadh stays at Cnoc àrsaidh the better part of a month after Ailig's burying and tells the new keeper that the pit's first flake of any new working shall go on being given free to whoever asks, as it always had, and that he will see to it himself that the custom does not lapse.

title: The hawk lintel at Àth mhòr
body: A hawk is carved on a lintel over a house door at Àth mhòr in the north, wings closed, head turned. It is the oldest carving of a hawk on the island, and of any bird.

title: The hawk carved into the lintel at Àth mhòr
body: Walking the far eastern circuit alone, Murchadh watches a young man of Àth mhòr cut a hawk into his father's door-lintel by firelight over three evenings, wings closed and the head turned back over the shoulder; the carver says only that the shape came to him whole one night and would not leave him alone until he had cut it, and no carrier ever hears of an earlier bird cut in wood or stone anywhere on Dia-thìr.

title: Wolves at Tobar fhiadhaich
body: At Tobar fhiadhaich wolves are buried whole and with care, laid on their sides as people are. No other beast is so buried in this age.

title: Murchadh sees the wolves buried at Tobar fhiadhaich
body: In his hundred and eighty-fifth year Murchadh comes upon a household at Tobar fhiadhaich burying a wolf on its side with its legs drawn up as in sleep; asked why, an old woman of the household says the wolf keeps its own dead on the high ground and has earned better than the ditch, a care they have never spoken of outside the household before.

title: Murchadh asks his father for the north
body: Murchadh comes south to Dùn ìseal and asks his father for the whole northern country Rathad na Spor runs through, which he has walked, he says, more times than any man living and knows better than any man living knows it.

title: The king refuses Murchadh the north
body: The king answers that the north is Dòmhnall's to hold, given him sixteen hundred years before and well kept since, and that a share once given is not taken back for a better claim that comes after it; Murchadh rides north again within the week without asking a second time.

title: The first grievance of Ailean's line
body: Murchadh rides out of Dùn ìseal with a face his father's household has not seen on him before, nearer pride than the young man's face he wore going north the first time, and close under the pride, by the telling of those who marked it, the first grievance the hill ever had cause to lay at a son of Ailean's own naming.

title: The high pastures fail at Dùn ìseal
body: A spring of near-ceaseless rain rots the high grazing at the root, and households begin killing beasts they would ordinarily have wintered, for want of anything left to feed them.

title: Sìleas opens the store within the bank by the mouth, not the herd
body: Sìleas Bhàn orders the grain-pits cut into Dùn ìseal's own earthwork opened to every household by the count of mouths at its hearth rather than by the size of its herd, the first time the store is shared by that measure; a wealthier herdsman rides up to protest it to her face, and she does not change the measure.

title: Sìleas Bhàn and the hungry years
body: Sìleas Bhàn, eighth of the Stone Kings, of the king's blood, holds Dùn ìseal through years of failed grazing. No deed is told of her but that she held, and the list goes on after her.

title: Households begin refilling the store unasked
body: With the grazing still short, households of Dùn ìseal's own ground begin returning grain to the bank's pits beyond what was drawn from them, a custom Sìleas Bhàn lets stand without ordering it, judging it will hold firmer for growing its own root.

title: The grazing recovers
body: The high pastures dry and thicken again within three years of their failing, as such lean spells generally did on that ground, though the store within the bank is not filled to its old level again for a decade.

title: The hunger at Baile chrom is first heard of at the hill
body: Word reaches Dùn ìseal, slow and uncertain, of two failed fishing seasons on the north-western shore at Baile chrom, of stores already gone to bark and boiled seaweed, and of graves being laid two deep for want of time to dig them singly.

title: The hunger at Baile chrom
body: Hunger comes to the settlement on the site of the north-western Baile chrom. Its pots are left full of boiled bark and seaweed, and its grave-rows are doubled. No older hunger on Dia-thìr is tied to a place.

title: The king rides north-west with grain
body: Ailean Mòr rides to the north-western coast himself with the first grain that can be spared, by a road that has never before carried him, and is gone the better part of a season; he returns saying nothing of what he found, save that every hill of the kingdom is to look to its own store before the next storm season.

title: Sìleas sends grain along the whole north-western coast
body: Sìleas Bhàn holds Dùn ìseal in the king's absence and sends three cartloads of grain and a small herd of goats after him, with instruction that they go to whichever hearths along that coast are worst served and not to Baile chrom alone, having heard the hunger reaches wider than one shore.

title: No household near Dùn ìseal again lets its store run low
body: Once the doubled grave-rows of Baile chrom are known at the hill, no household within a day's ride of Dùn ìseal again lets its own grain fall below a season's worth, whatever the grazing does, for fear of what might one day be asked of it.

title: The wells of Achadh shean run low
body: The wells of Achadh shean in the east fall a hand lower than any digger there remembers, a thing thought at first too small to trouble the hill with.

title: A shepherd's boy walks to Dùn ìseal to report the cracking banks
body: A boy of Achadh shean walks three days to Dùn ìseal on his own feet rather than trust the telling to a rider, to say that the field banks his grandfather raised have cracked from dryness for the first time in three generations; Sìleas Bhàn sends a rider east to look before sending any grain.

title: The springs of Achadh shean stop
body: The rider sent east returns saying the springs of Achadh shean have not merely run low but stopped outright, their whole visible flow gone at a season when they have never before failed within living telling.

title: The drought at Achadh shean
body: The springs of Achadh shean in the east run dry so long that the field banks are forsaken and grown over. When people return they cut new fields on another line.

title: The field banks of Achadh shean are forsaken
body: With the springs three years dry, the households of Achadh shean walk off their old field banks, leaving the dead barley standing in the row, and cut new fields on another line lower on the slope, where a lesser spring still runs thin but steady.

title: Sìleas refuses to have the dead field pulled down
body: Riding out to see the forsaken banks of Achadh shean, Sìleas Bhàn refuses her own rider's suggestion that they be levelled, saying a bank tells a household what the ground once gave and what it stopped giving, and is worth more standing than pulled down.

title: Sìleas asks the king what her deed will be
body: At Cruinneachadh an Àtha Sìleas Bhàn asks Ailean Mòr what the list will say she did, having herself set no boundary stone, fought no war and raided no shore; he tells her that four hundred years of not failing, where failing was always the easier road, is itself the deed the list will keep.

title: Sìleas Bhàn gives Dùn ìseal to Tormod Liath
body: In her five hundred and tenth year Sìleas Bhàn gives the hill to Tormod Liath, a son of Iain Dubh of thirteen hundred and seventy years, ordering the store within the bank counted before witnesses so the new holder takes it up knowing to the basket what it holds.

title: Tormod Liath keeps the grain-measure unchanged
body: In his first words as holder, Tormod Liath tells the households he will change nothing about the store within the bank, having watched it feed two hungers in his own lifetime and seeing no reason to improve on a measure that has already held.

title: Tormod mends the bank and the boundary marks
body: In his first seasons holding Dùn ìseal, Tormod Liath sets right what the hungry years let go: the silted ditch, the leaning palisade, and the boundary marks between the hill's fields and the households', blurred by two lean summers of each man taking what he could.

title: Tormod buries his eldest son
body: Tormod Liath's eldest son dies of years, the first of the three heirs Tormod outlives; the old holder stands at the burying still dark-haired, and is named by his own son's grandchildren as their grandfather's father.

title: The naming of the wind directions
body: The eight winds are named, and every Dia-thìreach sailor after uses the names. Their meaning is dark even to those who speak them, and they have never been changed.

title: Na h-Ochd Gaothan are named
body: Na h-Ochd Gaothan of the year, known before only by their feel, are given names all at once by no one the coasts can afterward name. Every coast that tells it uses the same eight names in the same order from that year on.

title: Fearchar Gobha brings the wind-names to Tormod
body: A salt-carrier of the hill, Fearchar Gobha, hears the eight wind-names at the coast fair and brings them up to Tormod Liath, who says only that a landholder has no business owning what belongs to the sea.

title: Eilidh born in the valleys under the hill
body: A daughter of the king's blood is born in the valleys under Dùn ìseal and named Eilidh; grey-eyed from her first year, she grows up at her own hearth with no thought of holding anything more.

title: Three brothers raise Clachan nan Gaoth at Ceann leathan
body: Aonghas, Dùghlas and Ailig mac Torcaill, brothers of the point, quarry eight stones from an outcrop above the landing and raise them in a ring, one for each named wind, so a sailor may lay a hand on the stone of the wind he wants before he puts out.

title: The wind-stones of Ceann leathan
body: Eight tall stones are set in a ring on the point at Ceann leathan, one for each of the named winds. Sailors of every later age touch the stone of the wind they want before they put out.

title: The crooked stone reset
body: One bad winter after Clachan nan Gaoth are first raised at Ceann leathan, the stone of the hardest offshore wind is found settled crooked and is dug out and reset on a footing of smaller stones, standing straighter and newer than its seven fellows ever after.

title: Tormod buries his second son on the western slope
body: Tormod Liath's second son, who held the hill's western grazing and never cared for the hall, is buried at his own asking on the slope where he herded, and Tormod says a man ought to be let choose his own ground if nothing else is left him to choose.

title: The wind-names carried to the islands
body: The eight wind-names are used on Eilean fhada as on the main island. The markers on its high point bear eight cut notches, one facing each way.

title: The wind-names cut into the rock of Eilean fhada
body: The people of Eilean fhada, off the northern cape, keep no ring of stones but cut the eight wind-names as notches into the rock of the island's highest ground, one facing each way, so a man lost in thick weather may find his bearing by touch.

title: Raghnall Ceannfhionn dies
body: Raghnall Ceannfhionn, who waded into the ford to strike the bargain of salt for wool, dies in his fourteen hundred and first year; the ford keeps its autumn meeting that year as every year, and the two hills send more wool and more salt than the bargain asks.

title: Tormod Liath
body: Tormod Liath, ninth of the Stone Kings, a grandson of the king, holds the hill so long that he outlives three heirs, and is remembered as old. In his time Dùn ìseal is given its second bank, and its ground is doubled.

title: Tormod paces out the second bank
body: Tormod Liath walks the line of Dùn ìseal's second bank himself through two winters before calling the households in to dig, taking in the low ground by the spring without losing the height needed for a watch-fire.

title: The households dig the second bank
body: The households of Dùn ìseal dig through a spring and a summer to raise the second bank, doubling the ground held within the hill's earth from some forty houses to very near a hundred.

title: Tormod buries his third son and tells him it does not hurt
body: The youngest and last of Tormod Liath's three sons dies asking his father, near the end, whether it hurts to be left each time; Tormod tells him no, the one lie the tellings of that hill ever charge against him.

title: Tormod goes fully grey
body: By his hundred and seventy-fifth year of holding, Tormod Liath is grey through, brows and beard with the rest, and the young of the hill, who never knew him dark, take him for the oldest thing on Dùn ìseal, older even than the second bank he raised.

title: The king raises Tormod from the mud at the gate
body: The king comes to Dùn ìseal's gate with a handful of his household and no word sent ahead; grey, stooped Tormod Liath kneels to him as every holder before him has knelt, and is raised again by a hand that has not aged since Tormod's father knelt the same way.

title: A child asks why the old man kneels
body: A granddaughter of Tormod's second son, watching from the bank, asks her mother why the young stranger lets the old holder kneel to him as at a common gate; her mother tells her that evening, by the fire, what the hill has long known and rarely says aloud.

title: The Dia-thìrich name
body: In this age the hill-folk begin to call themselves Dia-thìrich and the island Dia-thìr. The first use is not known; the eldest tellings take both names for granted. With the names goes the belief: they did not come; they were here.

title: Children begin to call themselves Dia-thìrich
body: The children of Dùn ìseal begin, unbidden by any elder, to call themselves Dia-thìrich and their island Dia-thìr, in place of hill-folk or the grove-born name Clann nan Dè; within a generation the old words fall out of use among the young.

title: Tormod is told the island's new name by a boy of seven
body: A boy of the new ground within the second bank tells Tormod Liath, asked what clan he is, that he is Dia-thìreach and that everyone is; Tormod answers only that it is a good enough name for a good enough island.

title: Ealag and Torcall Tochlair are promised by their households
body: Two households of the hill above Dùn ìseal, who share a slope and a spring, treat a match between Ealag and Torcall Tochlair as already settled. Torcall's mother carries the salt across to ask for it in the old way.

title: The salt is refused
body: Torcall's mother brings the salt back unaccepted. The elders of Ealag's household give her no reason, only that the match cannot be, and she comes home with her face set as it had never been set before.

title: The first forbidden marriage
body: A marriage between two lineages is forbidden, for a reason no surviving telling gives. Already the Dia-thìrich order themselves by blood, long before the coal gives them cause.

title: Torcall is turned away at every door
body: Torcall Tochlair goes himself to Ealag's father and her uncles and is told, in the same three words each time, that the marriage cannot be. None of them will say why, and he cannot tell whether none of them know it or all of them have sworn silence.

title: Ealag's mother weeps and will not say
body: Ealag asks her own mother for the reason and is told only to stop asking, and her mother weeps, which Ealag has never seen her do, not even at a burying.

title: Ealag given to a household of the ford
body: Ealag is married to Donnchadh, a fisher of the ford town, who asks for her honestly and does not learn of the earlier match for three years.

title: Torcall hears of the black hill in the east
body: Torcall Tochlair, restless at the coal-banks under the mountain, hears from traders of ground in the east with a look of coal about it, and begins asking the older diggers whether the vein is the island's only one.

title: Lines recited at the ford
body: At the ford gathering households begin to recite their lines aloud before any marriage is made, seven names back on either side. These are the first genealogies of the common households; only the Line of the Mason is older. None survives whole.

title: The lines first recited at the ford
body: Before any match is spoken at the fair, a household stands and gives its line aloud, seven names back on either side, so a forbidden blood may be named before the salt is carried. Ealag hears it and thinks of the four shut mouths that refused her.

title: Ealag tells Donnchadh of Torcall
body: That evening Ealag tells her husband of the match that was refused her. He says only that it explains a look she sometimes wears at fair-time, and asks nothing further.

title: Calum born to Eilidh
body: A son is born to Eilidh in the valleys under the hill and named Calum, dark from his birth; he will be the elder of her two sons and the one who stands where an heir stands.

title: Lachann agrees to go east with his brother
body: Torcall's younger brother Lachann, easier in temper but loyal to him, agrees to go east to the black hill with two other restless diggers, meaning to see Torcall satisfied and brought home again.

title: The first seeking of another vein
body: Diggers from Dùn ìseal open a trench on a hill near Cnoc dhubh in the east, seeking coal like the vein's. They leave it unfinished when two of them are crushed by a fall. The trench stays open, and what it would have found is not known.

title: Lachann buried at the trench's mouth
body: Torcall will not have his brother carried elsewhere and buries him where he fell, at the mouth of the trench on the black hill. The other man killed with him is carried home by his own people.

title: Torcall builds a shelter at the trench
body: When the other diggers pack their tools and go back to the coal-banks under the mountain, Torcall Tochlair stays, and builds himself a turf shelter at the trench's edge for the winter.

title: Word of Torcall reaches Ealag
body: A trader who stopped at the black hill brings word to the ford of a man sitting alone beside an open trench with his brother in the ground nearby, still saying he means to find the coal.

title: The stone that would not break
body: A second opening for a new vein is made elsewhere on the island and fails wholly: common rock, and nothing beneath it. So it is first known that the vein under the mountain is alone of its kind.

title: The saying of the vein's choosing begins to travel
body: After the second opening strikes only unbroken common stone, it is said across the island that the vein under the mountain is alone of its kind and chose its one place the way na Seachd Guail are said to have chosen theirs.

title: Ealag dies at the ford
body: Ealag dies in her own bed at the ford with her children about her, having lived her whole life after the refusal without the reason for it.

title: The will for a third opening goes out of the island
body: No elder forbids a third trench outright, but the wish for one fades everywhere at once, the way the wish for a refused match fades in two households without a word spoken between them.

title: A household gathers at the black hill's foot
body: Folk who come to the black hill for one reason or another begin to stay, since the ground is as good as any and the man who keeps the open trench asks nothing of them.

title: The prospecting ends
body: No one tries a third opening in this age. The Dia-thìrich hold that the vein chooses where it lies, and that the choice is not theirs to try.

title: Torcall Tochlair dies at the trench
body: Torcall Tochlair dies at the black hill and is buried beside his brother at the trench's mouth. The household he gathered keeps the ground and does not fill the trench in.

title: The first shared meal law
body: A custom arises, unwritten, that any household with food to spare shall share it before the storm season.

title: The shore-woman's catch carried in whole
body: A woman of the shore households at Dùn ìseal, whose net takes more mackerel than her family can eat or smoke before it turns, carries three baskets of it to the bank herself rather than let it spoil unshared. Tormod Liath comes down from the hall to help her set them down. After it the sharing before the storms needs no one to ask.

title: A holder shamed into doubling his own surplus
body: A holder of one of the near valleys mocks a household that brings little to the sharing. His neighbours say nothing against him, but the next year he brings in double his own surplus unasked. No reciter keeps his name.

title: Surplus shared at Dùn ìseal
body: At Dùn ìseal the sharing before the storms is done in the open: every household brings its surplus within the bank, and it is divided by the count of mouths. The custom has no earlier place that is known.

title: Beasag born at Àth shean
body: A daughter is born to a careful household at Àth shean, the ford below Dùn ìseal, some years after her father digs a grain pit under the byre floor against nothing he can name. Her mother dies bearing the last of her brothers three winters before the lean year that will end the household's place at the ford.

title: Lachlann born on An Cnoc Ruadh
body: A son is born in An Cnoc Ruadh's hall and named Lachlann, red-headed like so many of that line; he grows up wet to the knee on the lake shore and learns the salt-rake before the spear.

title: Oighrig born to a herder of the near slopes
body: A daughter is born to Dòmhnall, a herder of the near slopes above Tobar dhìreach with no kinship to Rìghrean na Cloiche, and named Oighrig; she grows up sitting her household's turns at the slab and will draw the white stone at three-and-thirty.

title: A lean storm season at Dùn ìseal
body: Failed grazing and short-headed barley along the near valleys, with three weeks lost to a wind that will not turn, make the leanest storm season since the sharing began. The division at the bank is thinner than any household remembers, and old people come to be counted though they have nothing to bring.

title: Beasag watches the division made by the count of mouths
body: Beasag, seventeen, is sent to Dùn ìseal with her household's share in the lean year and sees the sharing divided by the count of mouths: a widow with four children carries home more than she brought, and a boy holds his first full sack too long to trust it. She says nothing of her father's pit.

title: A household turned out at Àth shean
body: A household at Àth shean hides its spare grain in a pit under the floor and brings nothing to the sharing. When the pit is found the household is put out of the settlement with what it can carry. It is the first punishment under the custom that is remembered.

title: Beasag tells of her father's pit at the ford
body: In the first mild days after the storms break, a woman mending net on the bank at Àth shean asks Beasag idly whether her father's byre came through the lean year as thin as the rest. Beasag answers true: there is a pit under the floor, and he never brought it all in.

title: Tormod Liath sends to open the floor at Àth shean
body: Word of the hidden pit reaches Tormod Liath at Dùn ìseal by way of Àth shean's own holder. He asks only whether the girl told it of her own will, unbeaten and unbribed, and on being told she had, sends his men to open the floor.

title: The household of Àth shean put out with what it can carry
body: Grain enough for two households through the lean winter is found beneath the byre floor. Beasag's father is given until dark to take what his household can carry on its backs and to be off the ford's ground by morning: the first punishment under the sharing custom that is remembered.

title: Beasag's household settles east of the vein
body: After eleven days on the road, Beasag's father builds a house on a nameless slope east of the vein, where the king's blood holds no hall and claims no grazing, among households that went out a generation before for their own reasons. He digs no pit under this floor.

title: Sìleas Bhàn dies among her kin
body: Sìleas Bhàn, who opened the store within the bank by the count of mouths, dies among her own kin in the valley below the bank in her eight hundred and eightieth year; Tormod Liath comes down from the hall to stand at her burying.

title: Peigi born on An Cnoc Ruadh
body: A daughter is born to Lachlann Ruadh and named Peigi, black-haired and loud from her first night; she will meet her father's fosterling at the gate at fifteen and tell him he is too thin.

title: Tormod Liath dies at Dùn ìseal
body: Tormod Liath dies in his own hall, without wound or fever, in the three hundred and eightieth year of his holding, having outlived three heirs of his own body and buried each at the bank he built. Dùn ìseal mourns him the length of a season; scarcely a household on the hill remembers a holder before him.

title: Eilidh Ghlas takes up the hill
body: The holding of Dùn ìseal passes to Eilidh Ghlas, of the king's own blood, who has lived out those same generations in the valleys under the hill without thought of holding anything but her own hearth. She takes up the sharing custom with the hill itself, and weighs it at the bank herself in her first years.

title: Eilidh Ghlas asks after the pit at Àth shean
body: Before the bank is even swept for the season's grain, Eilidh Ghlas sends to Àth shean to ask after the pit still known by the name of the man who dug it. She is told it stands empty, and says only that this is well.

title: Calum Ciar stands where an heir stands
body: In the first sharing of his mother's own holding, Calum Ciar stands a pace behind Eilidh Ghlas's shoulder at the bank, and the ford takes notice of him for the first time. No one at Dùn ìseal afterward looks for another heir.

title: Eilidh weighs the old custom of the valleys
body: Eilidh Ghlas turns over, without acting on it, a custom she learned as a girl in the near valleys: that a household with two sons sometimes sends the younger to be raised at another hearth, so that he grows up loved rather than waiting on an inheritance not his.

title: The younger son born in a high river spring
body: A second son is born to Eilidh Ghlas at Dùn ìseal in a wet spring, when the river at Àth shean runs high enough to float the ford-stones. No reciter keeps his day, and none ever will.

title: Eilidh Ghlas
body: Eilidh Ghlas, tenth of the Stone Kings, of the king's blood, sends her younger son to the Red Hill to be fostered, the first fostering in either list. The son's name is not kept; only that he went, and that the peace of the ford held while he was there.

title: A boy who does not ask to ride out
body: Eilidh's younger son, six years old, watches his brother ride out with the men to renew the boundary stones and does not ask to go. His mother watches him a long while from the hall door and tells her steward that a house with only one door out of it is no house for a second son.

title: Word sent west to An Cnoc Ruadh
body: Eilidh Ghlas sends word to Lachlann Ruadh, holder of An Cnoc Ruadh, asking that he take her younger son to be raised in his household. She gives it out as a mother's wish that the boy learn a trade of his own; the ford's peace is served by it besides.

title: Calum Ciar counts the miles at the gate
body: On the morning his brother leaves for An Cnoc Ruadh, Calum Ciar stands long at the gate after the party is out of sight, and tells a groom who asks him in out of the wind that he is only counting how many days fifty miles there and back will take.

title: Eilidh's parting at Àth shean
body: Eilidh Ghlas walks with her son's party as far as Àth shean and kneels to his height at the turning of the roads, telling him he is not sent for any wrong of his, that An Cnoc Ruadh will be as much home to him as Dùn ìseal, and that she means to see him grown.

title: A mound left untouched on Rathad an t-Salainn
body: On the road west, the household man Donnchadh stops before a low green mound and will go no nearer to it, telling the boy only that it is older than the road and the salt trade. A wise traveller, he is told, lets such places lie as he lets a wasp's nest lie.

title: Rìonach's saying of the forked river
body: Turning off Rathad an t-Salainn for her own kin at Àth shean, Rìonach tells the fosterling that a household not his own by birth is no loss to him but a doubling, as a forked river becomes two whole rivers rather than two lesser ones.

title: The fosterling comes to An Cnoc Ruadh
body: Eilidh Ghlas's younger son comes down to the western lake shore at evening and is met at the gate by Lachlann Ruadh and his daughter Peigi, who tells her father plainly that he is too thin and will need feeding, and carries in his one bundle herself.

title: Lachlann forbids the naming of a king's son
body: Lachlann Ruadh tells his household that the fosterling shall be called no king's son and no king's grandson, but a boy of the ford's people come to learn a trade, and warns his daughter Peigi he will hear of it if she names him otherwise again.

title: Lachlann Ruadh takes the fosterling
body: Lachlann Ruadh, holder of the Red Hill, takes the son of Eilidh Ghlas into his house. For it he is named Lachlann an Altraim, 'Lachlann of the fostering', and the Red Hill list calls him so more often than by his own name.

title: Calum Ciar given the boundary stones
body: Calum Ciar is given the judging of the near valleys' boundary stones, the first trust of its kind laid on him, and settles a dispute between two herders over a shifted marker with a plainness his mother is said to have approved of.

title: The fosterling first put out on the lake
body: The fosterling is let out on Loch chrom in a boat for the first time, and comes back to An Cnoc Ruadh wet through and pleased with himself, word of it carried east along Rathad an t-Salainn to Dùn ìseal by the carriers who walk it.

title: Eilidh Ghlas visits An Cnoc Ruadh
body: Eilidh Ghlas comes to An Cnoc Ruadh as Lachlann Ruadh's guest and sits at his own board four days, asking after the tallies and the weather as she asks after her son. Walking with her son to the western point of the lake, she tells him she will not come again for some years.

title: The fosterling rakes salt without breaking the crust
body: Lachlann Ruadh puts a salt-rake into the fosterling's hands on the drying platform above Loch chrom and shows him the turn of the wrist his own family has kept for generations. By the fourth stroke the boy lifts a clean sheet of crust whole, and Peigi Dhubh tells him it is better than she managed her own first year.

title: An Cnoc Ruadh list begins to call Lachlann of the fostering
body: In these years An Cnoc Ruadh's reciters take up the habit of naming Lachlann Ruadh also Lachlann an Altraim, Lachlann of the fostering, until in time the second name is given by the list where the first once stood, and is never afterward unsaid.

title: Beathag gives up the list of the slab's turns
body: Beathag, who has kept the household order of the slab's night watch eleven years, says at the Samhain gathering that she will keep the list no longer, after a household comes two nights running to a turn already missed. Thirty-one households now stand on it, too many for one memory to hold true.

title: The families agree to choose the slab's keeper by lot
body: At the slab's own clearing the families of Tobar dhìreach and the near valleys meet to settle the watch. An old man of the gathering proposes a single keeper chosen by lot, to hold the slab until death or infirmity, rather than turns by household. No vote is taken; the silence that follows is read as agreement.

title: Oighrig, first keeper by lot
body: The families who watch the slab agree to choose one keeper at a time by lot, and no longer to take turns by household. The first lot falls to a woman called Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill, and she keeps the slab for the rest of her life.

title: The lot falls to Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill
body: At the next full dark, thirty-one households send one member each to draw from a bag of thirty pebbles and one marked white. The lot falls to Oighrig, a herder's daughter of three-and-thirty, who carries the marked stone in her belt from that night for the rest of her life.

title: Oighrig's father speaks of the shared name
body: Walking home from the drawing, Oighrig's father Dòmhnall, a herder of the near slopes with no kinship to Rìghrean na Cloiche, tells her she will spend the rest of her keeping answering travellers who mistake her for blood of Dòmhnall Clachach, the second of that name to hold the north.

title: The keepers' house
body: A house is built beside the slab at Tobar dhìreach for the holder of the lot, its door facing the stone. It is rebuilt on the same footing many times. It is the first building on Dia-thìr made only to be near the vein.

title: Taigh na Lice raised at Tobar dhìreach
body: The families of the near valleys build Oighrig a house on the clearing's edge above the slab, its door set to face the stone and no other way, the first building on Dia-thìr raised for no reason but to stand near the vein.

title: Oighrig sits her first winter alone by the slab
body: Moved into the new house at the first hard frost, Oighrig finds the keeper's long unbroken watch harder than any turn shared with her own household, and begins to notice things about the stain and the stone's temper that a thousand years of turned watches had never set down.

title: The stone cup
body: Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill has a cup ground out of grey stone to the size of her own cupped hand, that the handful of coal may be the same for every household. The cup is carried round the hill settlements. Whether it outlasts the age is not known.

title: Oighrig comes to Niocol Snaidhear with her cupped hand
body: In her third year of keeping, Oighrig goes to the stone-worker Niocol Snaidhear and sets her own hand on his bench, cupped as for water, asking for a cup of grey stone that will hold exactly what it holds, so that no household's handful of coal runs bigger than another's by the accident of whose palm measures it.

title: The first two stone cups crack in the grinding
body: Niocol Snaidhear loses a first cup to a hidden vein in the stone and a second to a hair-crack struck too hard near its finishing, and keeps the flawed second on his bench through the grinding of the third as a thing to learn the shape of a mistake by.

title: Niocol finishes the cup ground to Oighrig's hand
body: After eleven sittings across two summers, Niocol Snaidhear finishes a cup of grey stone fitted to Oighrig's hand, veined faintly white, holding exactly what her two cupped hands together cannot quite hold. She says the hand it copies is not her own but the hand of every hearth; Niocol begins a second cup as a copy before he is asked.

title: Word of the stone cup travels the near valleys
body: News of Oighrig's cup and the trouble it answers reaches stone-workers at three other places within the year: a woman at Àth gharbh, an old man at Achadh dhìreach, and a household at Cnoc chaol, each asking to grind a copy against it.

title: The stone cup copied
body: Copies of the keeper's cup are ground at Àth gharbh, Achadh dhìreach and Cnoc chaol, each tried against the first by filling it with water. Thereafter the hill settlements measure the coal with one measure.

title: Oighrig carries the first cup to Àth gharbh, Achadh dhìreach and Cnoc chaol
body: Oighrig walks the near valleys over a year with the first cup wrapped in wool, testing each new copy against it by pouring water from one to the other on a flat stone, and sending two cups at Achadh dhìreach and one at Cnoc chaol back to the wheel when the levels do not match.

title: The four cups are ground true at Àth gharbh, Achadh dhìreach and Cnoc chaol
body: The copies of the stone cup are finished: quickest at Àth gharbh, where the worker measures against Niocol's cup throughout rather than a hand alone; slowest at Achadh dhìreach, an old man's hands steadied by his grandson through the last evenings; and, despite two false starts, fastest of all begun at Cnoc chaol.

title: The meeting of the cups
body: The keeper's cup and its three copies are carried to a spring on the moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach, set side by side on a flat stone and filled from the spring in turn. The place is called Coinneachadh nan Cupan, the meeting of the cups. The hill settlements return to it whenever a cup is broken and a new one must be tried.

title: Coinneachadh nan Cupan on the moor
body: At a nameless spring on the moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach, chosen because it lies equal walking from all four places and belongs to no one household, the four keepers of the cups fill each from the same water on a flat stone and pass every cup down the line for each hand to weigh. The water stands level in all four; the place is called from that morning Coinneachadh nan Cupan.

title: The hills measure the coal with one measure
body: From the year of Coinneachadh nan Cupan, the households from the slopes above Tobar dhìreach to the poor ground of Cnoc chaol measure their handful of the vein's coal by the one cup and its three copies, and not by the hand that happens to do the measuring, a change the reciters afterward give no more than a single line.

title: Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill dies keeping the slab
body: Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill keeps the slab for the rest of her life, as the lot gave it her, and that rest is shorter than anyone at the clearing looked for: she dies in Taigh na Lice in the winter after Coinneachadh nan Cupan, and the families ask that a new lot be drawn.

title: Gilleasbuig Beag takes coal
body: A keeper by lot, Gilleasbuig Beag, is found with a basket of broken coal from the vein in his own house. The households of the hills sit in judgement at the slab, row him out to Eilean chrom, and leave him there without a boat. He is the first known to be exiled for the vein.

title: The lot falls to Gilleasbuig Beag
body: The bag of pebbles is filled again and passed among the households near the crack. The white stone comes out in the hand of Gilleasbuig Beag, a broad, quiet man known for mending roofs and cutting hazel, who goes pale rather than glad at what his open hand shows.

title: A basket found under the bed-place
body: A kinswoman of Gilleasbuig, in his house on another errand, lifts a cloth expecting food and finds a basket of broken coal from the vein, more than any hand is owed by the handful. She says nothing that day, but tells her husband before she sleeps, and within three days the near valley knows.

title: Gilleasbuig does not deny it
body: Called to the clearing, Gilleasbuig Beag owns the basket at once and says he took the coal against a hard winter, for an old mother who sleeps cold, and for no other use. He asks, when the judgement is given, what the stone gains by the coal's return that his mother does not lose by going without it.

title: The families judge Gilleasbuig by silence
body: The households argue long in the cold before an old woman of Cnoc chaol says what none of the near families will say first: that the vein was never any one hearth's to keep behind a cloth, however true the love that took it. The clearing's silence, held past any voice rising to answer it, stands as the judgement.

title: Gilleasbuig Beag rowed to Eilean chrom
body: Three men of the near households row Gilleasbuig Beag out to Eilean chrom and put him ashore, then pull back to open water and leave him without a boat to return in. He is the first anyone remembers exiled for the vein.

title: A fire seen three nights on Eilean chrom
body: The near coast watches a small fire on Eilean chrom's low rise the first night, smaller the second, and a coal's worth of red at dusk the third, gone before full dark. No fire is seen there again, and no boat is sent to learn why.

title: The basket set inside Taigh na Lice
body: The kinswoman who found the coal carries the basket to Taigh na Lice at Tobar dhìreach and sets it under its cloth just inside the door. No household proposes burning it; it was not theirs to burn before Gilleasbuig took it, and the judgement has settled that it never will be.

title: The lot falls to Giorsal Bhàn
body: A new lot is drawn from the same bag that gave the stone to Oighrig and then to Gilleasbuig, and this time it is Giorsal Bhàn's hand that opens on the white pebble. She closes her hand on it and says she will keep it, and moves into Taigh na Lice before the month is out.

title: The coal returned to the crack
body: The coal from Gilleasbuig Beag's house is neither burned nor kept. The keeper after him carries it back to the slab and lays it beneath, piece by piece. The tellings make much of it: the coal went home.

title: Giorsal lays the coal back under the slab
body: On a still morning near the year's turn, Giorsal Bhàn kneels at the slab's lower edge and presses the broken coal back into the gap between stone and earth, piece by piece, returning a second day to finish it, until the basket holds nothing at all.

title: "The coal went home"
body: By the summer after Giorsal Bhàn empties the basket into the slab's edge, the four words are already going round the near valley as if they had always been there: that the coal went home. No one near the crack can afterward say who spoke them first.

title: Eilean chrom left to itself
body: The island stands ungrazed and unfished through the years after Gilleasbuig Beag's exile. Children of the near coast are told not to ask about the island with the spring on it, and are given the same short answer when they ask anyway.

title: Calum Ciar asks for the lot
body: Calum Ciar, the elder son of Eilidh Ghlas and eleventh of the Stone Kings, asks that the keeper's lot be drawn at Dùn ìseal in his sight. The households at the slab refuse him. The list sets down the refusal, which is more than it sets down of most things.

title: Calum Ciar comes to the clearing
body: Calum Ciar, elder son of Eilidh Ghlas and eleventh to hold Dùn ìseal under the king, walks up the valley to the slab and asks that the next lot be drawn at Dùn ìseal in his own sight, so the hill may see the vein's lot drawn as honestly as the hill's own.

title: The families refuse Calum Ciar
body: The households near the crack answer Calum Ciar with the same held silence they gave Gilleasbuig Beag: the lot has been drawn at the slab since the custom began and will go on being drawn there, in the sight of whoever near the crack cares to watch. Calum Ciar thanks them and does not argue it.

title: Calum Ciar puts the question to the king
body: At the ford that summer, Calum Ciar carries the same question to the king. The king hears him without anger or haste and says only that the slab is older than the hill, and older than the grove of his own crowning, and that he will not overrule so old a thing for the asking of a man not two hundred years in the world.

title: The kings and the keepers
body: After the refusal of Calum Ciar the lot is still drawn at the slab. The holders of the hill rule the grazing and the gatherings under the king, but not the vein, and the king does not overrule the slab. The line between the two holds for the rest of the age. It is not yet written anywhere.

title: The line between hill and slab holds unwritten
body: Calum Ciar goes home from the ford and asks nothing more of it. The hill rules the grazing and calls the gatherings, answering to the king for both; the keepers rule the vein, answering to no one the telling can name. The line is sworn to in no words either side writes down, and it holds.

title: A' Ghaoth Dhubh
body: A storm called A' Ghaoth Dhubh, the Black Wind, strips the thatch from every house on the east coast from Cuan ruadh to Ceann chiar. Of all storms it is the eldest whose name is kept.

title: The sharing holds after the Black Wind
body: The settlements of the east coast feed the people of Cuan ruadh through a whole winter out of their shared surplus. None on that coast is known to die of hunger that season.

title: A' Ghaoth Dhubh strips the east coast
body: A storm out of the south-east strikes before dawn with almost no warning, stripping the thatch from every roof between Cuan ruadh and Ceann chiar and driving three unhauled boats onto the rocks below the headland. No one of that coast dies in it, though many households lose stores, shelter and boats within a single day.

title: The coast's fishing fails before winter begins
body: Of Cuan ruadh's eleven boats, four are broken past mending and a fifth needs a new keel; granaries stand open to the sky along the whole stripped coast. A fishing that has never in memory failed outright fails that winter for want of boats and stores enough to work it.

title: The coast names the storm A' Ghaoth Dhubh
body: The eldest of that coast, having no name ready when the storm struck, name it afterward for the ash-dark sky it leaves behind for three days. No reciter of the hill amends the name; every storm to strike that shore since is measured against it.

title: Inland valleys hear of the coast's ruin
body: A trader who meant to buy salt fish at Cuan ruadh finds instead a shore of broken boats and bare roof-trees, and carries word of it a day and more west to valleys that had never before troubled themselves over that coast's weather.

title: The valleys send grain to Cuan ruadh unasked
body: Single households send what they can spare because a neighbour has already sent something, until the scatter of gifts grows too large for any one house to account for, and the valleys' holders agree to weigh and send it on by the count of mouths, as the sharing is kept at Dùn ìseal, though none there had been taught the custom directly.

title: The beacon at Baile ìseal
body: A fire is built on the eastern cape where Taigh-solais Baile ìseal now stands, kept by the households of the coast in turn. It is lit to bring boats home in a storm, the tellings say, and not to warn them off.

title: The sharing reaches the east coast
body: Grain, salted meat and wool for roofing come down to Cuan ruadh through the winter on carts and cattle-backs, weighed by mouths and given without reckoning who at the coast has lost most. No household of that coast starves; the coast calls the custom only the bringing-in, or the help.

title: Lìleas begins to watch the dark return of the boats
body: One-and-twenty that hard winter, with her father's hand maimed and the household's boat unfit to swim, Lìleas of Cuan ruadh spends idle hours on the shingle and comes to notice what the coast has never put into words: that a boat coming home after dark has nothing to steer the last stretch by but memory and the sound of the surf.

title: Lìleas's household agrees to the fire
body: Lìleas puts the keeping of a fire on the cape east of the village to her own household over a thin meal; her father, no longer trusting his maimed hand on a line, sees no harm in it and asks only that she carry the work herself.

title: The eastern fire is first kept
body: Lìleas and her younger brother carry driftwood and peat up the cape through a month of short winter days and build the fire in a stone-walled pit, driving flame and smoke seaward. She keeps it alone through nights that find no boat needing it, and more than one household of the village climbs the cape only to sit an hour with her.

title: The beacon at Muileann bheag
body: A second shore-fire is kept on the north coast, on the point where Taigh-solais Muileann bheag stands now. Under the tower the ash goes down through three yards of fire-reddened soil.

title: The beacon at Àth dhearg
body: Households of the north-east coast keep a fire on the cape where Taigh-solais Àth dhearg now stands, and cut steps up to it from the shore. The steps are narrower than those at Seann Bhral, and less worn.

title: Word of the eastern fire travels the coast roads
body: Traders and travellers carry word of the fire on Cuan ruadh's cape along the roads faster than its own light could reach, and coasts that have suffered their own bad weather begin to want fires of their own.

title: A fire is raised on the northern point
body: On ground already scorched black by older shore-fires, the households of the hardest-running coast raise a fire that burns steadier from its first season, having Lìleas's year of trial to learn by before laying their own wood.

title: Seathan mac Pheadair keeps the north-eastern fire
body: On the cape where the passage to the deeper water runs narrowest, a man named Seathan mac Pheadair takes up the keeping of a fire much as Lìleas had, and cuts a stroke on a stone at its edge for every ship's light he sees pass safe by it.

title: The beacon at Tobar dhearg
body: A fire is kept for the boats of the south coast on the southern cape where Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg stands. With Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag and Àth dhearg the coasts of the island are lit at five points.

title: The southern cape completes the five fires
body: Last of the four new fires and by every account the surest, the households of the southern cape raise theirs on a mound of stacked stone breast-high, clear of the spray. With the older fire on the Baile chrom headland, the coasts of Dia-thìr are now lit at five points.

title: A reciter names them the five fires
body: Before the southern mound is even finished, a reciter of that coast says that a boat lost off any shore of Dia-thìr now has a fire somewhere within its sight to steer toward, and names the five together the five fires, a name the coast keeps on every telling since.

title: A boat is brought home to the eastern fire
body: Blown off its own water by a wind that will not hold steady, a boat out of a coast two villages north finds the coast of Dia-thìr only by Lìleas's fire, burning high on the cape with no house near it. The crew comes ashore whole, and Lìleas tells the captain the fire is kept for whichever boat needs it, no more for him than for any other.

title: The Sea-Watcher seen from Seann Skell
body: Four watchers on the north-western tower at Seann Skell see a back as long as three boats rise and go under off the point. It is the first sighting of the Sea-Watcher tied to a named place and a count of witnesses.

title: Wreckage in the western water
body: For a season planks of stitched boats, broken small, wash up along the western shore below the waters where raiders are afterwards seen. No bodies come with them, and no settlement on that coast lacks a boat.

title: The watchers see the long back in the water
body: Four men keeping the tower at Seann Skell watch a back long as three boats rise off the point in the failing light and go under without a sound. Their four tellings differ in every small particular but agree on the length and the silence.

title: Word of the sighting runs round the bay
body: The tale of the tower's watch grows a head and a neck by the time it has gone twice round the bay of Seann Skell, though the old women of that coast say only that the sea shows itself when it chooses and take no boat off the water for the telling.

title: Stitched planks come ashore south of Seann Skell
body: Through a season the wrack south of the tower gives up narrow stitched planks from more than one hull, shaped for open water and like nothing built on that coast, with not one scrap of cord, tool or bone to say what rode in them.

title: No household will claim the wreck
body: Asked along the shore, no household admits to a boat of its own building broken among the planks, nor lacks a man, woman or child it cannot otherwise account for; the wreck stays a wreck with no name and no mourner.

title: Micheil Beag lays the planks against his wall
body: A fisherman of that coast, Micheil Beag, gathers the stitched wood along one wall and pieces two curved lengths of hull back into shape, finding boats narrower and longer in the beam than any the coast builds for its own close fishing.

title: Anndra Breac comes to the wall of planks
body: Anndra Breac, a teller who has walked the western shore twenty years and more without a household of his own, hears Micheil Beag out and returns to look at the planking again by firelight more than once before the season turns.

title: Anndra shapes a fourth telling
body: Turning the planks and the tower's tale over through the winter, Anndra comes to think a boat lost whole but for its wood argues not a wreck close to shore but a crossing once made, long before any telling now kept remembers the making of it.

title: The coast hears him out without agreeing
body: Anndra tries the telling first on households that have fed him twenty years running; none of them denies it outright, and an old woman near Seann Skell tells him a tale a man cannot leave alone wants telling somewhere it will be properly heard.

title: Anndra Breac says 'we came'
body: At the ford gathering Anndra Breac, a teller of the western coast, recites a telling in which the people came to Dia-thìr over the sea. The households of the hills shout him down, and he is put out of the ford for the rest of his life. His telling is not kept; only the memory that he told it.

title: Anndra Breac tells the crossing at the ford
body: At the yearly gathering, by the largest fire he can get a footing at, Anndra Breac tells a telling in which the hill-folk crossed the sea in boats once and lost more of themselves to the crossing than any telling now remembers.

title: The crowd shouts him down
body: An old man of a hill household calls out that no teller says the hill-folk came from anywhere, for they were always here, and others take up the shout until Anndra's own voice can no longer be heard over the fire.

title: Every hearth of Dia-thìr closes to him
body: No household strikes him and none needs to; by the roads home from the ford it is already understood that Anndra Breac is not to be fed at a hill hearth again, and by the following spring not one has.

title: The king laughs once and falls quiet
body: Standing near enough his own fire to hear the telling, the king laughs low at some point in it those nearest him cannot agree on afterward, does not join the shouting nor still it, and is seen quiet the rest of that evening in a way his own kin know to read.

title: The king will not choose between the tellings
body: Asked afterward by a woman of his own kin whether the teller spoke true, the king answers only that he has heard many tellings of where his own people came from and has never troubled to choose one over another.

title: The doctrine said at the column
body: After Anndra Breac, the saying cut on the column at Cnoc ghorm is spoken aloud at the opening of the ford gathering: we did not come; we were here. From this time it is said as a rule, and not only held as a belief.

title: The saying is spoken at the opening of the gathering
body: The gathering at the ford opens for the first time with the saying of Calbh Cnoc ghorm spoken aloud before any business begins, we did not come, we were here, a thing said together from that year rather than kept only in each hearth's own quiet belief.

title: Anndra Breac walks south along the western strand
body: Seen once more below the tower at Seann Skell, walking the strand where the stitched planks still lie against Micheil Beag's wall, Anndra Breac walks on and does not look back; no teller of that coast claims to have fed, spoken to or buried him after.

title: The keepers of the Ros dhomhain rock
body: The tide-rock at Ros dhomhain passes to Seònaid Mhòr, who cuts her marks in pairs, one for high water and one for low. Her pairs can be read still. The keepers after her go back to single marks.

title: A third tide-rock at Inis thais
body: Households at Inis thais cut their own high-water marks on the harbour rock, at the interval of Ros dhomhain. So three rocks are kept side by side. None tells why the interval is what it is.

title: Seònaid Mhòr cuts paired marks at Ros dhomhain
body: The keeper of the Ros dhomhain tide-rock takes to cutting two strokes for every tide instead of one, a mark for the water's highest reach and a shorter mark beside it for its lowest ebb, so that whoever reads the rock after her has the whole of the water's motion and not only its rising.

title: The spacing of the marks travels without its reasoning
body: Households at Inis thais's own harbour, hearing only that Ros dhomhain's keeper cuts her marks at a certain interval, begin cutting their own high-water marks at that same spacing on a rock of their own, though none of them can say why that width and no other.

title: Peigi Dhubh calls for a landing of laid stone
body: At the household's board, Lachlann Ruadh's daughter says plainly that a hill whose wealth now travels by water deserves better than an open shingle beach a winter tide can rearrange. Her father agrees, and the households of An Cnoc Ruadh give a season's labour to the work.

title: Ros dhomhain grows
body: Ros dhomhain becomes the greatest settlement on the shores of Loch chrom, some sixty houses round the tide-rock. Its people fish now from boats and not from the shore.

title: The stone landing is set at the river-mouth
body: Course on course of quarried stone is laid where the fresh water of the lake meets the tide from the sea, until a boat can come alongside at any state of the water without a hand needed to haul it clear of the mud: An Cnoc Ruadh's first way onto open water that does not depend on a beach's mercy.

title: Lachlann Ruadh falls ill
body: A chill taken wading the shallows to right a boat settles in Lachlann an Altraim's chest and will not lift with the spring. He is five-and-sixty years old, an age An Cnoc Ruadh reckons past complaint for a man who has spent his whole life wet to the knee in cold water.

title: Lachlann asks that the fostering be ended
body: On one of his last evenings Lachlann tells his daughter that a fostering kept a season too long stops being a kindness and becomes only a habit no one has ended, and asks her not to let her own fondness be the reason the peace of the ford goes one day longer without its proper marking.

title: Lachlann Ruadh dies at five-and-sixty
body: He dies in the hall he was born in, his daughter's hand in his own, the household gathered at the door with no closer claim on the bedside than the years they gave the hill. He held An Cnoc Ruadh one-and-sixty years.

title: Peigi Dhubh holds An Cnoc Ruadh at forty
body: She sits down at the board the morning after her father's burial and asks for the tallies before she asks for anything else. An Cnoc Ruadh's own steward says afterward that she keeps them straighter than her father ever did.

title: The Red Hill's harbour
body: The households of the Red Hill build a landing of laid stone at the river-mouth below the hill, where the harbour of Cathair dhearg is now. It is the Red Hill's first way onto the water, and by the lake and the Abhainn gheal to the sea.

title: Peigi Dhubh of the Red Hill
body: Peigi Dhubh holds the Red Hill after Lachlann an Altraim. She sends the fostered son of Dùn ìseal home grown, with gifts of salt, and the peace of the ford holds a generation more.

title: Houses draw in round the rock and the landing
body: Boats from harbours further down the coast begin putting in at the new landing rather than carrying on to open beaches, and the scattered houses of that shore draw in closer round the tide-rock and the stone together until some sixty stand there, their people fishing now from boats of their own building.

title: The foster-son returns
body: The son of Eilidh Ghlas comes home from the Red Hill to Dùn ìseal, bringing the salt-songs of the west. The Stone Kings' list gives him no name and no reign; he is remembered only as the one who went.

title: Peigi tells the fosterling he is to go home
body: Walking the new stone landing with him in the last light of an evening, Peigi says her father was right, and that she means to send him home before the year turns, with salt enough for a household to carry as gift and not as trade, so the hill of Dùn ìseal will know he is sent back with honour.

title: Seònaid Mhòr cuts a last pair of marks for him
body: On the evening before the train leaves, the keeper of the tide-rock cuts one more pair of marks at the rock's edge, though the tide calls for none, and will not say plainly what they are for beyond that the rock has marked every tide of his years there and should mark the last of them too.

title: The first songs kept
body: The salt-songs of the south and west are sung at the raking of the pans. They are the oldest songs on Dia-thìr whose words are said to survive: a refrain of four lines, which no one can now wholly construe.

title: Bone pipes at Cnoc àrsaidh
body: Pipes of hollow bird-bone, bored with four holes, are made in a house at the southern Cnoc àrsaidh near the panther road. They are the oldest instruments of the island.

title: The panthers turn back
body: The great cats come down the panther road near Imrich nam Pantar and turn back at the foothills without crossing. The hill-folk read it for a hard winter and store double. The winter is hard.

title: Gilleonan bores the first bone pipes
body: At Cnoc àrsaidh, Gilleonan bores four holes along a hollow bird-bone and finds a note he can raise and lower at will; children of three households gather to hear him play, the first instrument the island's tellers count as more than a horn blown flat.

title: Three cats turn back at the pass
body: Watchers along Imrich nam Pantar see three great cats, on three different days, halt at the throat of the highest pass and turn back south rather than finish the crossing every household's memory says they always finish.

title: The households along the road store double
body: Reading the cats' turning for a kinder ground left behind and a harder winter ahead, the households nearest the pass lay in double against a season no cat that year would risk crossing into, and go short of nothing before the thaw.

title: Iain drives cattle onto Imrich nam Pantar
body: With the household's grazing run thin, Iain of Muileann bhàn takes four men and forty head of thin cattle up into the passes against the custom that keeps the crossing season's road clear of herds, meaning to bring them down fattened within the week.

title: The cattle lost in the passes
body: Herders from Muileann bhàn drive cattle into the passes out of season, against the custom of the crossing. The panthers take thirty head in a night, and the herders come down with nothing.

title: The foster-son of Dùn ìseal comes home
body: He walks Rathad an t-Salainn east with a train of laden pack-beasts and three of An Cnoc Ruadh's household, and comes in sight of the hill of Rìghrean na Cloiche on the seventh evening, four-and-twenty years after he first walked the same road west at six years old.

title: Calum Ciar does not know his own brother
body: Meeting An Cnoc Ruadh's train at the gate in his mother's stead, Calum Ciar asks the fosterling which of the household he might be, a lake wind and four-and-twenty years having left nothing in him his brother's eye could fasten on as kin.

title: Eilidh Ghlas knows her son at the door
body: Carried out to the hall door, Eilidh speaks her younger son's name before he has said a word to tell her who he is, and weeps and holds him a long while before she lets even her elder son greet him in turn.

title: The salt refrain is sung at the pans of Baile ghorm
body: At the fires of the salt-rakers he teaches, without meaning to teach anything, the four-line refrain sung at the crust on An Cnoc Ruadh's own lake shore. An old raker keeps it whole from a single hearing, and it runs on afterward at the sea-shore pans in words An Cnoc Ruadh itself can no longer wholly construe.

title: Rìghrean na Cloiche' list keeps him no name
body: When the reciters after Eilidh set down her reign and her sons, Calum Ciar takes his place among the holders as every holder before him; of the one who went to An Cnoc Ruadh and came home grown, no year, no reign and no deed is written, and the list stands as if she bore only the one son.

title: The panthers take thirty head in the night
body: On the fourth night a string of cats, the last and largest of that year's crossing, comes down on the herd; by first light thirty of the forty head are taken or scattered beyond finding.

title: Iain is lamed in the dark
body: Throwing himself clear of a claw he never clearly sees, Iain twists his leg under him against a hidden stone; it sets crooked at the hip, and he walks from that winter with a stick and a roll to one side.

title: Baile dhomhain cuts the first season's sign
body: The households of Baile dhomhain begin cutting a mark into every gatepost at the start of the crossing season and scraping it away at its close, the first mark the island's tellers know cut for a season rather than for any single event.

title: Caol bheag names its boats for the winds
body: The fishing households of Caol bheag fix the custom of naming each boat for the wind it is built to fish in, holding a boat unlucky under any other wind and never giving a drowned boat's name again.

title: A wind-name is cut at Seann Chwen
body: A cutter of that household sets one of Na h-Ochd Gaothan' names beside Seann-Dhaoine' own marks on the great boulder at Seann Chwen, choosing that stone, by his own word, because the name wanted a stone already old.

title: A family takes up the old burial ground unasked
body: Kin new to that country begin clearing the thorn from the old burial ground's rows each spring though none of their own dead lie there, and within a few years every household near it has come to trust the keeping to them alone.

title: The panther season kept at Baile dhomhain
