body: At Baile dhomhain in the south the households cut a sign on their gateposts at the start of the crossing season and scrape it off at its end. It is the first mark made on the island for a season.

title: The wind-stone at Seann Chwen
body: One of the eight wind-names is cut in the Dia-thìreach manner on a boulder at the central Seann Chwen, over an older mark of the Seann-Dhaoine. In few places do the marks of the two peoples touch.

title: Boats named for the winds
body: The fishing households of Caol bheag, who fish the north coast from the mouth of the Abhainn ghorm, name their boats for the winds they fish in. A boat named for the wrong wind is held unlucky, and the name of a boat that sinks is never given again.

title: The Tuam keepers
body: A family dwelling by Tuam Cnoc dhìreach takes on the clearing of thorn from the old graves. They bury none of their own there. They only keep it.

title: A grave at Tuam opened
body: Diggers laying a new row at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach break into a grave older than any they knew, lined with slabs cut in the manner of the Seann-Dhaoine. They close it and move the row, and none opens that grave again.

title: Diggers break into a slab-lined grave
body: Cutting a new row further back than any before it, the keepers' own diggers break into an older grave lined close with cut slabs in the manner of Seann-Dhaoine; they close it as carefully as they opened it and move the row a spear's length off.

title: No digger tries the older grave again
body: The keeping family's eldest holds that a ground kept for the dead does not want its keepers asking after graves it was never given to keep, and no digger of that ground troubles the older grave a second time.

title: Pilgrims at Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
body: People begin to walk to the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and sit a night at the line of the trees without entering. Their small fires, each of a single night, lie all along the edge.

title: Pilgrims begin sitting at Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
body: People from households that have never before walked so far begin coming singly and in pairs to sit a single night at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, keeping a small fire that burns out before morning, and go home saying only that the night leaves them quieter.

title: Settlers from An Cnoc Ruadh raise the first house at Cnoc bheag
body: Households come down from An Cnoc Ruadh to build at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, taking timber only from the river's far side and never from the unclaimed wood, a line later marked by a row of unhewn stones.

title: A child lost in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
body: A child of the settlement at Cnoc bheag goes past the line of stones into Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag and is not found. The searchers stop at the stones, and the telling does not blame them.

title: A child of Cnoc bheag is lost past the stones
body: A boy not yet seven goes missing near the line of stones at Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag's edge; the settlement and its neighbours search three days into the wood without one sign of him.

title: Iain among the searchers who stop at the stones
body: Lame still from the passes, Iain of Muileann bhàn joins the search at Cnoc bheag and is the first to say aloud that a wood no household will fell or build nearer than its own river is not a wood that gives back what it takes; the searchers stop at the line of stones, and no teller lays the stopping at their door.

title: The first house at Cnoc bheag
body: Settlers from the Red Hill build at Cnoc bheag, near the edge of the forest. They take their timber from the far side of the river, and never from the unclaimed wood.

title: The spring at Muileann ruadh
body: Pilgrims come in numbers to the warm springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, and a ring of shelters is built there. Here is set the eldest healing-tale of Dia-thìr: a herder came lame and walked home.

title: Iain goes to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
body: Seven-and-twenty years lame, and told by a neighbour of a warm water under the mountain that has eased other travellers' old hurts, Iain walks south on his stick and sits in the pool at first light, the heat working into the crooked hip as no binding ever had.

title: Iain walks home whole; the cure-tale is set
body: Iain stays three days at the warm water and walks the road home to Muileann bhàn on his own two legs without the stick, in half the days the journey south had cost him; his own household, seeing him come up the rise, takes him at first for a stranger. The tale kept of it is the oldest cure the springs are told for: he came lame, and he walked home.

title: The Hollow Man seen again
body: Two herders passing the Doire uaine hills after dark see a figure walk the ridge with no breath showing in the cold. They had no fire lit, and so, the telling says, they lived.

title: Two herders see Marbh-bheò on the ridge
body: Caught by dark on the way home, two herders near Marbh-bheò's hills see a shape walk the ridge above them showing no breath in the bitter cold, though their own hangs white before them; they had lit no fire that evening, and so, the telling says, they lived.

title: The covered hearth spreads
body: The covered hearth, pit-dug and roofed, spreads from the Doire uaine hills to the settlements about Muileann chiar. From this comes the later rule that no open fire is lit on those slopes after dark.

title: Peigi Dhubh dies on An Cnoc Ruadh
body: Peigi Dhubh, who laid the stone landing and kept the tallies straighter than her father, dies on An Cnoc Ruadh in her seventy-sixth year, having held it five-and-thirty years; her boats go out the morning after her burying as she asked.

title: The covered hearth spreads and the night rule hardens
body: The pit-dug, stone-lidded hearth spreads from Marbh-bheò's hills toward the settlements nearer Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, and it hardens there into a rule no council ever set: no open fire is lit on those slopes after dark.

title: Settlers at Caol mhòr
body: Dia-thìreach households settle at Caol mhòr in the north-west, on the strait where the Seann-Dhaoine once hunted seal. They find the old middens and build on them.

title: Caol mhòr's settlers set aside the marked midden stones
body: Households raising walls from Seann-Dhaoine' shell midden at Caol mhòr will not turn a stone that carries a mark, cut or worn, and lay those aside in an unmortared line along the shore, so that two kinds of wall stand side by side there ever after.

title: Somhairle walks the ground at Baile chrom
body: Somhairle finds the resettled fields at Baile chrom already byred and welled, and Donnchadh Ruadh shows him the old field-marks still standing half sunk beneath the new grass, ploughed by hands no household there now names aloud.

title: Settlers at Baile chrom in the north-west
body: Households from Cnoc ghorm settle again the ground at Baile chrom that the old hunger had emptied. They dig their storage pits deeper than any others on the coast.

title: The last thicket on Rathad an t-Salainn is cut through
body: Carriers weary of the long way round cut through the last unbroken stand of thorn and birch on Rathad an t-Salainn to the north-west, so that Muileann àrsaidh stands a full day nearer the pans of Baile ghorm than it had ever stood before.

title: The first bank is turned east of the old workings
body: Settlers pushing toward the rising country dig a ditch and raise the spoil behind it at Dùn thais, a ring of earth built without any word sent from Dùn ìseal and without any word sent back once it stood.

title: Muileann àrsaidh settled
body: Houses are built on the stream at Muileann àrsaidh in the north-west. Their flint comes from Cnoc àrsaidh, and their salt from the south, carried the length of the island.

title: Fire clears the heavy ground at Achadh chaol
body: Across three dry summers the households of Achadh chaol burn back the old scrub a field's width at a time and plough the black ground while the ash still holds its warmth, taking the first year a crop the older fields to the west had not equalled in a generation.

title: The last course is set on Cuan ruadh's wall
body: The households of Cuan ruadh finish laying stone to the eaves the whole circuit of the settlement, the first roofs on that coast built to stand against wind rather than merely to be raised again once it has passed.

title: A well is opened within Cathair fhada's bank
body: Cathair fhada digs and lines a well inside its own earthwork, so that a household need not send its water-carriers down to the shore while a storm still has teeth in it.

title: The salt road to the north-west
body: A salt road runs from the pans of Baile ghorm by the ford gathering to the north-west. At Muileann àrsaidh the salt costs three times its price at the pans, and is paid for in flint and seal-skins.

title: Caol ruadh's fishers mark the strait's channels
body: The fishers of the narrow strait take to tying woven buoys over the deep channels where the current runs hardest, a small custom that spreads along the coast in a carrier's mouth the way the paired tide-marks spread before it.

title: Doire ghlas settled
body: Households settle under the oaks at Doire ghlas in the north. The settlement grows in rings, each built outside the last as the wood is cleared back.

title: Households come down to Doire ghlas
body: Families out of the near valleys settle in the grove where the king kept his seven nights, drawn by its shelter and its old cleared paths, and mark timber in the oaks themselves for the first of their new byres.

title: Somhairle asks the household to spare three oaks
body: Finding the three oldest trunks of the grove marked for the axe, Somhairle asks Fearchar mac Ailig's household to take their roof-beams elsewhere, giving no reason beyond that his father once set six pots beneath those particular trees.

title: The three oaks are spared
body: The household cuts its beams instead from younger growth a short walk east and leaves the three old trunks standing at the centre of the new settlement, ringed within a generation by houses that call the place only the ring under the oaks.

title: The east settled at Dùn thais
body: The hill-folk push east and build a banked enclosure at Dùn thais, on a hill above good grazing. It is the first stronghold of the Dia-thìrich away from Dùn ìseal and the Red Hill.

title: Achadh chaol cleared
body: Fields are cleared at Achadh chaol in the east by fire and by picking stones. The picked stones are laid in banks round each field, and those banks bound the fields still.

title: Somhairle finds grey in his beard
body: A cheese-seller on the road through the near valleys remarks on the grey coming into Somhairle's beard, and he finds at a still pool that she has told him true: the first lines his face has shown in two thousand four hundred and thirty-five years.

title: Beathan sees his father's face has changed
body: Coming on Somhairle unexpectedly at the slab, Beathan stops in the doorway before he crosses it, having seen in his father's face the beginning of an ageing neither of them has yet spoken of aloud.

title: Cuan ruadh rebuilt
body: Cuan ruadh, stripped by the Black Wind, is rebuilt in stone to the height of the eaves. It is the first settlement of the east coast to build its walls against the wind and not only the cold.

title: Cathair fhada on the south coast
body: Cathair fhada is founded on the south coast, between the old Seann Dunn and Seann Chwen. It draws its water from a well the Seann-Dhaoine dug, and never speaks of where the well came from.

title: Caol ruadh on the southern strait
body: Fishing households settle Caol ruadh on the south coast and take the cod of the strait on long lines. Their middens are the first on the south coast to hold more fish than shell.

title: Murchadh rides north to hold the plain
body: The king sends his son Murchadh north with sixty households to hold the northern plain in his name, the first of the king's sons given ground beyond the settled valleys to keep rather than merely to pass through.

title: Baile Mòr mhòr in the north
body: Houses are built at Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern plain, round a spring that never freezes. At its height it has some eighty houses, a great place for the age.

title: Baile Mòr mhòr rises round the spring that never freezes
body: Murchadh raises his hall on a rise above a spring that runs clear through every winter, and the households of the plain name the place Baile Mòr mhòr before it has earned the size of the name; within four centuries it stands eighty houses, the largest place north of An Cnoc Ruadh.

title: Sheep-households settle Baile gharbh
body: Households take up the stony ground north-east of Murchadh's spring, keep sheep where the land will bear nothing heavier, and send their wool south along the coast road to Cruinneachadh an Àtha rather than north to Murchadh's own granary.

title: Baile fhiadhaich settled among the boar-thickets
body: Settlers build on the western coast where the boars run heaviest, hang tusks over their doors, and take boar for their chief meat; the island comes to know a man of that place by his gait, from a lifetime of walking ground a boar might break from underfoot.

title: Baile gharbh in the north-east
body: Households settle the rough ground at Baile gharbh and live by sheep, not cattle. Their wool goes south along the coast to the ford gathering.

title: Cuan shean settled beside the old landing
body: Households take up a harbour beside a stone landing built by hands none of them can name, older than any wall near it, and use it as they find it rather than mend it, out of the caution settlers keep wherever Seann-Dhaoine' work still stands.

title: Eithne nic Ailein is born
body: A daughter is born to the king in the near valleys and named Eithne; she grows quicker of tongue than most of her father's blood troubles to be, and comes north, in time, to hold ground of her own rather than sit idle at any hearth.

title: Baile fhiadhaich on the west coast
body: Settlers build at Baile fhiadhaich on the western coast, where boars run in the thickets. They hang boar tusks over their doors, and boar is their chief meat for the rest of the age.

title: The first of Murchadh's eleven sons is born
body: The eldest of eleven sons is born to Murchadh over the better part of three centuries; each, coming of an age to want it, is given a corner of the plain to hold under his father rather than a place idle at his hearth.

title: Dùn chrom is raised with its bank facing two ways
body: Herders wanting the bank to face south and quarrymen wanting it to face north raise, between them, a single crooked earthwork that answers both wants at once and satisfies neither fully, and the bent fort stands from its first year with a name that fits it more ways than its builders meant.

title: Cuan shean settled
body: Dia-thìreach households take up the harbour at Cuan shean on the west coast, beside an old landing of unknown builders, and use the landing without mending it.

title: Eilidh Ghlas dies
body: Eilidh Ghlas, who sent her younger son west to be raised and knew him at the door when he came home, dies in her seven hundred and thirtieth year; both her sons stand at her burying, and the list keeps only one of them.

title: Tobar dhearg rises round the red well
body: The keepers of a beacon on the southern cape build at last round a well whose water runs faintly red from the rock, and their settlement grows into the greatest place on that coast, its fire burning nightly for ships that have learned to watch for it.

title: Dùn chrom raised
body: A banked hill-fort is raised at Dùn chrom in the midst of the island, between the Red Hill and the hills of the vein. Its bank faces both ways.

title: The holders of Dùn chrom and Dùn thais quarrel over which way a bank should face
body: Ruadhan Beag of Dùn chrom and the holder of Dùn thais fall into two winters of hard words over which way a bank ought to face, until Murchadh rides to hear them and leaves the ditch as it stands, finding a hundred years without an enemy a better argument than either holder makes against it.

title: Beathan mac Shomhairle dies at Tobar dhìreach
body: Beathan, son of Somhairle, who sat his nights at the slab since before Murchadh was born, dies in his two thousand two hundred and thirteenth year, the oldest death yet counted among the king's kin; the households of the north, hearing the number, begin for the first time to reckon what it may mean to outlive a holder's holder.

title: Cathair mhòr below the old outpost
body: Households settle on the ground below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, where Cathair mhòr now stands. They take no stone from the ruin above them, though it is the nearest quarry.

title: Eithne's households name the ground below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire Cathair mhòr
body: Settlers below a broken watch-tower ask Eithne, then a hundred and forty-four years old, to lay out their fields, and she stays; her households name the place Cathair mhòr, the great city, out of hope rather than size, and take no stone from the ruin above them.

title: Households come to Cnoc naomh for its spring
body: Settlers take up a hill already called, by no teller then living able to say why, the holy hill, and keep its water and the fact of its holiness together without asking more of either.

title: Muileann naomh is founded on piles over the marsh
body: The first houses of Muileann naomh stand on driven piles over standing marsh water between Tobar dhearg and the old Seann Skell, and are afterward moved to firm ground a bowshot inland once the piles prove the footing sound, keeping the name the marsh first gave them.

title: Cnoc naomh
body: Households come to settle on a hill for its spring, and the hill is already called Cnoc naomh, the holy hill. Why, is not known.

title: The king takes back the western valleys from Murchadh
body: After three hundred years in Murchadh's keeping, the king takes back the poorer western valleys of the northern plain and gives them to a grandson of An Cnoc Ruadh's line, saying only that the ground had grown crowded enough to want a nearer hand; Murchadh does not argue it, and the plain stops speaking of it within the year.

title: Tobar dhearg on the southern cape
body: The keepers of the beacon at Tobar dhearg build their settlement on the cape itself, round a well whose water runs reddish from the rock. It becomes the greatest place on the south coast.

title: Calum Ciar dies at Dùn ìseal
body: Calum Ciar, eleventh to hold Dùn ìseal under the king, dies in his seven hundred and eleventh year, having asked the slab for its lot once and never asked again; the king buries him on the hill beside his mother.

title: Muileann naomh founded
body: Muileann naomh is founded near the south coast, between the beacon at Tobar dhearg and the old Seann Skell. Its first houses stand on stilts over a marsh, and are afterwards moved to firm ground.

title: Diorbhail born at Tobar dhìreach
body: A daughter is born to a household of the watch at Tobar dhìreach and named Diorbhail; she will say her own line back before she can tie a shoe, and carry Sloinneadh a' Chlachair after Somhairle.

title: Diorbhail says her own line before she can tie a shoe
body: A child of Tobar dhìreach not yet three years old says her line back four generations at her mother's fire, for the pleasure of the saying and not because she is asked, and the households of Na Glinn Àrda begin to remark on her the way a valley remarks on any child who does an ordinary thing early.

title: Somhairle first sits Diorbhail by the slab
body: Somhairle takes the seven-year-old Diorbhail up to the slab for a morning, on no more of an asking than that her mother has no need of her, and gives her the small tellings that ring the Line rather than the Line itself, holding that a thing given too soon to too young a head is given badly.

title: The summons to An Cruinneachadh Mòr reaches the north
body: Riders of the king's own household bring word to Baile Mòr mhòr that every holder of every share of the island is to come to a gathering at the ford of salt and wool greater than any before it; Murchadh sends word to his sons and to Eithne, and rides south himself with sixty of his household.

title: An Cnoc Ruadh's salt-traders walk to An Cruinneachadh Mòr
body: Word goes out along every road that Cruinneachadh an Àtha in the three thousandth year since the grove will be kept greater than any before it. Households of An Cnoc Ruadh's lake shore, among them An Cnoc Ruadh girl and her mother, walk the fourteen miles down with their salt wrapped against the damp.

title: The great gathering at the ford
body: In the height of his days Ailean Mòr keeps a gathering at the ford of the salt and wool. The holders of the hill, the Red Hill, the salt shore, the north and the west set their hands in his. Some four hundred of his own blood stand about him, children and their children, more than the reciters can name in a night. Only the households east of the vein send no one.

title: The three grounds of the ford run together
body: More households come in than the ford's three grounds, downstream, upstream and the rise beyond the river, were ever laid out to hold, until by the second morning no one can any longer say which bank belongs to whom, and a child sent for water is an hour finding her way back.

title: Amber, pots and flint change hands at the ford
body: Potters of the north-west, a stranger from the far west with strings of drilled amber, and carriers of eastern flint trade the first day of An Cruinneachadh Mòr through, while households from opposite ends of the crowd sit down together to weigh what a marriage between their children might be worth.

title: The reciters mark the three thousandth year since the grove
body: An old reciter of the hill tells those at his fire that the year is the three thousandth since the grove was lit, and that word of the count has been carried out along every road that summer, drawing to the ford households who had never before troubled to send anyone to an ordinary gathering.

title: The crowd opens for the king unbidden
body: On the second morning the king comes down the hill road dressed as any herdsman, and the whole crowd between the road and the river opens a way for him without a word called, old people stepping back from the path with their eyes down as from nothing else at the gathering.

title: An Cnoc Ruadh's new holder is still called by his father's name
body: Among the five who wade out to put their hands between the king's, An Cnoc Ruadh's own holder is so newly come to his hall that half the crowd on the bank still names him for his father before catching themselves.

title: Somhairle stands nearest the king in the rings
body: Somhairle takes his place at the king's left hand in the river as the rings of the king's blood go in, two thousand nine hundred and sixty-two years old that summer and looking, those at the ford say afterward, every year of it.

title: Murchadh is pointed out among the king's blood
body: Murchadh, who holds the northern plain for his father and has by then eleven sons of his own scattered among the rings, is pointed out by name on the bank, a head taller than most beside him and looking, past his twelve hundredth year, no older than a young man.

title: Eithne stands young-faced in the outer ring
body: Eithne, not yet three hundred years old and looking a girl of twenty, stands laughing among the outer rings of the king's blood, named to the girl of An Cnoc Ruadh by a woman of the ford who knows the lines by heart.

title: The reciters reckon four hundred of the king's blood
body: The naming of the king's children and their children runs from midday to sundown and is not finished when the light fails; word passes along the bank that the reciters have counted some four hundred of his blood standing in the river that day, more than at any gathering before it.

title: A boy of the west asks whether it is one family
body: A boy of a western household, standing beside An Cnoc Ruadh girl at the bank while the naming goes on, asks her whether all of that in the water is truly one family, and neither child can find a plainer answer to give the other.

title: The east's absence is remarked and let go
body: Women of An Cnoc Ruadh note at the fire that no household from east of the vein has come to the gathering a second year running, turn the matter over a little while without an answer, and let it go with the fine weather, unremembered again within the hour.

title: An Cnoc Ruadh girl trails her hand in the warm ford
body: When the gathering has gone back to its fires and the king stands alone a while in the emptied ford at dusk, An Cnoc Ruadh girl, nearest the water of anyone left on the bank, finds it warm as bath-water round his legs and sees it smoke downstream of him in the last light.

title: A basket-weavers' boy tries the slab and turns back to his creels
body: A cousin of Diorbhail's goes up to the slab with her twice out of curiosity and finds he can make no sense of the names, choosing to learn the weaving of a creel that holds water instead. Neither thinks less of the other, and it stands as one more fact of the valleys: that the slab takes some and lets others alone.

title: Diorbhail catches a gap between two tellings
body: Testing her own memory against a household's telling of itself at the ordinary fires, Diorbhail finds a name kept differently from the way the Line keeps it and brings both versions to Somhairle rather than choose between them, and he settles which telling holds truer and tells her the reason for it.

title: Somhairle says at the fire he may not sit many more Samhains
body: At a Samhain fire before the whole round of the watch-households, Somhairle says plainly that he does not know how many more such nights he will sit among them, and the gathering falls silent around him, having never before heard him say such a thing of himself.

title: Somhairle gives Diorbhail Sloinneadh a' Chlachair whole
body: Over a single night at the watch-fire, with Beathan's son sitting the turn beside them, Somhairle says the whole Sloinneadh a' Chlachair through twice without a name out of place, the same way it was given to him and to Beathan before her, and sets her own name at its foot when he is done.

title: The valleys turn to Diorbhail's fire before Somhairle's
body: After the giving, households of Na Glinn Àrda begin bringing their children's names to Diorbhail's fire rather than Somhairle's, the way a valley turns by degrees from an old well to a new one dug beside it, the old well no less good for the turning.

title: Somhairle's face is likened to a withered apple
body: An old woman of the watch-households, seeing Somhairle at a distance one Bealltainn, says he has come to look like a withered apple left too long on the sill. The saying travels the valleys and sticks to him, so that in time the households speak of him by it as easily as by his own name.

title: Somhairle asks Diorbhail what waits for a man with no hall
body: At a fire with no one else near enough to hear, Somhairle tells Diorbhail the one thing his own father never told him: that he does not know what waits for one of the grove's blood who took no wife of the king's giving and no share of the kingdom, having no hall to be carried into when his years run out.

title: Beathan's son clears the path for Somhairle's stick
body: In Somhairle's last seasons, Beathan's son walks up before each Samhain to clear fallen branches from the path so the old man's stick will not catch in the dark, and sits longer at the slab on the nights Somhairle climbs to it, though no household asks this of him.

title: Somhairle mac Ailein dies
body: Somhairle mac Ailein, a son of Ailean Mòr born in his father's sixty-second year, dies in the high valleys at two thousand nine hundred and eighty-seven years, before his father. His line lives among Clann na Ceiste and holds no share of the hill. In each generation after him the long years are shorter.

title: Beathan's son finds Somhairle dead against the slab
body: In the season the valleys keep for turning peat, Beathan's son finds Somhairle sitting against the slab in the grey of a morning, his stick fallen just out of reach, with no mark on him anywhere; word goes down to Dùn ìseal before noon on the fastest pony the round can put under a boy.

title: The king buries Somhairle and keeps a night's vigil
body: The king comes up on foot the last two miles, buries his son with his own two hands beside the slab, and sits on the turf afterward with his arms round his knees until an old reciter comes to ask, well after dark, whether he will come in to the fire.

title: Beathan's son takes up the whole watch at the slab
body: With no household troubling to make it formal, Beathan's son takes the watch at the slab as his own to keep entire, as his father had kept it before Somhairle first divided the watching from the reciting between two hands.

title: Ceann mhin on the south-eastern shore
body: The south-eastern Ceann mhin is settled near Làrach an Dùin. Its people are the first to live in sight of the fortress ruin, and they will not go up to it.

title: Diorbhail keeps the Line by mouth and takes no share for it
body: Diorbhail says the whole Line through twice each Samhain to any of the watch-households who will hear it, adding each year's names to its foot and setting none of it down on leaf or hide, and takes no share from any hall for the keeping, as Somhairle held she must.

title: Ceann mhin's people will not climb to the ruin
body: The households settled in sight of Làrach an Dùin ruin on the headland build their houses with their doors to the sea and their backs to the broken walls, and will not carry off the good dressed stone lying loose there for the taking, an old woman of that shore saying a wall raised by other hands keeps its own quarrel.

title: The smiths of the southern Seann Skell beat out hooks faster than the sea wears them
body: Within a few generations of its resettling, the old harbour of the south becomes the busiest quay on that whole coast, boats going out on every tide and coming home heavy, and its smiths kept at the forge from first light beating out fish-hooks the fishing cannot outlast.

title: Achadh shean sinks its well before it breaks a furrow
body: The households returning to the fields cracked by the long drought sink a new well deep into the rock before they plant a single seed, and tell it after as a lesson to their children: dig first, plant after, a well proved in a dry summer being worth more than an early harvest.

title: Seann Skell of the south
body: Dia-thìreach households take up the old harbour at the southern Seann Skell and keep its old name. Within a few generations it is the busiest landing on the south coast.

title: A boy of Inis mhin is lost among the egg-ledges
body: A boy climbing after eggs is caught by dusk on a shelf below the cliff's highest nests, unhurt but unable to climb either way, and is brought up by torchlight on a rope woven that same night; afterward no one of that settlement works the cliffs alone, two to a rope by custom rather than any law spoken.

title: Raonaid born to the king on the eastern shore
body: A daughter is born to the king by a wife of the eastern shore and named Raonaid; quick of eye and slow to anger, she will be the half-sister Ìomhar Dearg loves best of all his father's many children, and the hearth he comes home to.

title: The first cairn rises above the fold at Muileann chaol
body: When the head of one of the settling households dies, his kin carry stones up the slope above the cattle-fold and raise the first cairn there, one stone laid at a time by whoever had known him; within a lifetime the slope holds as many small heaps of stone as the fold below holds cattle in a good year.

title: Achadh shean resettled
body: Households return to Achadh shean after the drought and cut new fields on the higher ground. They sink a deep well first and plant after, and the well does not fail again in this age.

title: Fearchar Bacach dies at Dùn ìseal
body: Fearchar Bacach, who has held Dùn ìseal for the king since he was lamed in the passes long before, dies quietly in his own bed at three thousand one hundred and thirty years of age; his house keeps the hill after him without any household troubling to remark that it is being kept.

title: Raonaid nic Ailein weds on the eastern shore
body: Raonaid nic Ailein, a daughter of the king born to a wife of the eastern shore, marries a herdsman of Fearchar's line from the river-lands below Dùn ìseal, known on that shore better by his flocks than by his name; her house there is afterward the hearth her half-brother Ìomhar Dearg comes back to between his wanderings.

title: Baile Mòr ruadh settles ground its people call empty
body: Households raise a broad red-earthed rise into Baile Mòr ruadh, a morning's walk from the old middens of Seann Dunn, calling the ground around them empty though the middens plainly say otherwise, and dig into nothing of what lies there.

title: Inis mhin settled
body: A few households settle at Inis mhin on the eastern coast. They live by the eggs and birds of the cliffs, and trade feathers inland.

title: A shepherd's flock will not cross the worn path at Làrach an Teampaill
body: A shepherd wakes from a sun-warmed sleep to find his whole flock standing stock still along the path worn round Làrach an Teampaill, none grazing, none straying past its edge, and drives them home without letting a hoof cross it, telling after that his sheep had more sense of the place than he did.

title: Ìomhar is born to the king and called Dearg for his hair
body: A son is born to the king in the south and named Ìomhar, called Dearg for hair redder than his father's or his brothers', who grows up about the southern shores and the eastern marches asking, before his first century is out, why a man may not simply be given ground and left to hold it.

title: Muileann chaol on its hill
body: Households settle on the hill at Muileann chaol, above the upper reaches of the rivers. Where the library stands now there is a cattle-fold.

title: Cairns on the hill at Muileann chaol
body: At Muileann chaol a cairn is raised for each head of a household at death, on the slope above the fold. By the end of the age some forty stand there.

title: Dòmhnall Clachach dies in the north country
body: Dòmhnall Clachach, sent north from Dùn ìseal more than three thousand years before and known there only as the stone-cutter's son, dies among people who never troubled themselves with what he had once been, at three thousand three hundred and eight years of age; word of it reaches the hill a full season after the burying.

title: Baile Mòr ruadh in the east
body: Baile Mòr ruadh grows up near the eastern Seann Dunn, on land its people call empty. The middens of Seann Dunn lie a morning's walk away, and the settlers do not dig into them.

title: The temple ruin avoided
body: The Dia-thìrich of the eastern hills pass Làrach an Teampaill without stopping and take no stone from it. A path is worn round it at a distance.

title: Ceann leathan's contests
body: At Ceann leathan the gathering by the wind-stones ends with wrestling and the lifting of stones. The heaviest, a black boulder, lies on the point still, and few have raised it.

title: Alasdair Làidir takes every fall of the contests at three-and-twenty
body: At the yearly contests below Clachan nan Gaoth of Ceann leathan, a young herdsman's son named Alasdair Làidir throws every man who stands against him from first light to last, the youngest ever known to do it, and is given by custom the first try at Clach a' Neirt that has never once been raised.

title: A grey stranger lifts the black boulder at Ceann leathan
body: After Alasdair Làidir's strength fails against it, an unknown grey-haired traveller steps from the watching crowd, sets his hands to Clach a' Neirt and raises it to his knees, then sets it down again gently rather than dropping it, and walks off the headland refusing to give any name the reciters might carry.

title: The tale of the lifted stone wears smooth at other fires
body: Carried from hearth to hearth along the southern coast, the tale of the grey stranger gains, within a few winters, a taller stranger, a one-handed lift and, at one fire near the southern Seann Skell, hands said to glow like a smith's iron, an embellishment Alasdair Làidir spends the rest of his life correcting wherever he hears it repeated.

title: The ford gathering grows
body: The ford gathering at Muileann òg now draws households from every coast. Its ground is parted by custom: the salt people downstream, the hill people upstream, the flint people on the far bank.

title: An old woman at the ford sets a matching tale beside Alasdair's doubted one
body: At Cruinneachadh an Àtha, crowded that year, an old man past his wrestling years tells, once more, of the stone lifted and gently set down at Ceann leathan; a grey-haired woman at the same fire answers his young doubters not by taking his side but by recalling a near-identical telling she heard thirty years before, from a different mouth entirely, at a fire near the southern Seann Skell.

title: Stone axes from the north
body: Axes of polished green stone from a quarry near Àth àrsaidh in the north-west are carried all over the island. They are too fine for work; most are laid unused in graves or under house floors.

title: Ìomhar Dearg wants a green axe for use, not for a grave
body: At a wake in the north-west, Ìomhar Dearg turns over the dead man's green axe before it goes under the turf and asks the son, plainly, for one of his own to carry and use, having buried enough kin himself to want a tool that earns its keep before it earns its grave.

title: The cutters of Àth àrsaidh turn Ìomhar away
body: An old cutter at the quarry tells Ìomhar Dearg that no green axe was ever cut to be swung, only shown, and that a man wanting an edge for work should go to a common smith and leave the green stone to the graves it is already promised to.

title: Ìomhar's grey axe outlives forty years of use
body: Ìomhar Dearg has a common smith cut him a plain grey axe that same winter, and uses it, reground more than once, for the better part of forty years before the head cracks on a misjudged root and he buries it himself in the ground it first turned.

title: The quarry at Àth àrsaidh
body: The green-stone quarry at Àth àrsaidh is worked by a few households who trade in nothing else, and the chips about it lie knee-deep. Before the age ends the quarry is forsaken, and the axes cease.

title: The last cutter of Àth àrsaidh dies without an apprentice
body: The seam of true green stone runs thin under every cut the households of Àth àrsaidh try, and the last cutter who still holds the old skill dies that year with no apprentice behind him, his own sons having gone to herding rather than a stone that no longer pays for the teaching.

title: The moor takes the north
body: The oak falls back, as the pollen in the bog under Doire ghlas shows. Heather, birch and bog-moss spread over the northern lowlands, and the groves that give the north its many Doire names shrink to the sheltered valleys, where they stand yet. In the north this is remembered as the time the winters lengthened.

title: The oak-groves of the north shrink to the sheltered valleys
body: About Doire ghlas and the low ground north of it, heather, birch and bog-moss spread over ground the oak had held unchallenged for longer than any household's reckoning, and the groves that gave the north its many doire-names draw back to valleys the wind cannot reach.

title: Stepping-stones cross Abhainn fhionn dry-shod
body: A household below the willow flats lays flat stones across the shallowest bend of Abhainn fhionn one summer's low water at a time, until within two generations a man may cross the whole width stone to stone in every season but true flood, the first made river-crossing the island has seen.

title: The river crossings of Abhainn fhionn
body: Stepping-stones are laid across Abhainn fhionn at its shallows, the first made crossing of any river on the island. They are older than the first bridges, and in places lie beneath them.

title: A drowning at the fords of Abhainn chaol
body: A spate on Abhainn chaol takes a party of twelve crossing its fords with salt. Thereafter none crosses there in the wet season.

title: Twelve are taken at the fords of Abhainn chaol
body: A spate with no warning a slower rise would have given takes a party of twelve crossing with salt at the fords of Abhainn chaol; five bodies go to their own kin, four unclaimed to the nearest household willing to dig, and three are never found.

title: Ìomhar comes two days too late to the drowning
body: Word reaches Ìomhar Dearg two days' walk south of Abhainn chaol and he comes as fast as the road allows, arriving to a river already fallen back to its ordinary height and the households of both banks already burying what could be found; no household crosses those fords in the wet season after.

title: Niall is born to Raonaid on the eastern shore
body: Raonaid nic Ailein bears a son on the eastern shore in a colder autumn than the last three running; her half-brother Ìomhar Dearg finds more of her quickness than of his own long line in the child's first evening.

title: The Black Wind remembered at Ceann chiar
body: The people of Ceann chiar, rebuilding after the Black Wind, set a stone in the midst of their settlement and cut on it a mark for every house lost: twenty-two.

title: Ceann chiar cuts two-and-twenty marks for A' Ghaoth Dhubh
body: Rebuilding after A' Ghaoth Dhubh that scattered their roofs a generation before, the households of Ceann chiar set a stone in their new-laid houses and cut a plain stroke for every house the wind took, two-and-twenty marks in a row with no names beside them.

title: A dry year on the eastern plain
body: The rivers of the eastern plain run low for a whole summer, and the households of Dùn ìseal and Muileann bhàn drive their cattle to the warm springs to drink. The shared surplus holds, and no deaths are counted.

title: A dry summer is answered by the shared surplus
body: The rivers of the eastern plain run so low one summer that Dùn ìseal and Muileann bhàn drive their cattle to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh to drink; the surplus each household had kept against such a year holds long enough that no death is counted for the thirst of it.

title: A second wave on the south coast
body: The sea comes in again over the low ground at Cnoc chaol, less far than before. The new houses stand higher on the slope, and none is lost.

title: A lesser wave comes in at Cnoc chaol
body: The sea rises again over the low ground at Cnoc chaol, less far than the wave the coast still tells of; the new houses built higher on the slope since that first wave take no loss, the water finding only empty byres to carry off.

title: The ground shakes at Cill ghlas again
body: The old crack at Cill ghlas moves again, and the spring shifts back uphill. The line of white stones is broken in two places, and is laid again.

title: The crack at Gleann na Scoltaidh moves again
body: The old crack in the ground shifts once more, moving the spring back uphill and breaking the line of white stones that marks the danger in two places; the households walk out with fresh stone and lay the line again exactly as their grandmothers laid it the first time.

title: Dùghall born to Ìomhar Dearg
body: A son is born to Ìomhar Dearg and named Dùghall, a grave, red-haired child with none of his cousin Niall's laughter in him; Ìomhar, near seven hundred years old, carries him on his wanderings before the boy can walk.

title: Cnoc bheag under the Carragh
body: Households settle on the bank of the Abhainn ìseal at Cnoc bheag, a short walk from Carragh Cnoc bheag. They set their houses so that no door faces the stone.

title: Households settle at Cnoc bheag with no door facing the stone
body: A generation settles on the bank of Abhainn ìseal a short walk from the standing stone at Cnoc bheag, and sets its houses, by no law anyone can name, so that no door among them faces the stone; every household built after keeps the same pattern unquestioned.

title: The seal rocks of Inis bhàn
body: The households of Inis bhàn on the lower Abhainn ìseal take seals from the skerries off the river mouth by agreement, one household to a rock. A rock taken out of turn is the commonest quarrel in their tellings.

title: Inis bhàn settles the seal-rocks by the tally of the turn
body: The households by the seal-rocks off the river mouth at Inis bhàn take one rock to a household in its own turn, kept on notched sticks; a rock taken out of turn is the coast's commonest quarrel, settled always by counting the tally aloud rather than raised voices.

title: Ìomhar Dearg asks the king for ground of his own
body: Nearly eight hundred years into a wandering right that let him sit at any hearth on the island, Ìomhar Dearg asks the king, on the hill, for ground held in his own name rather than his blood's, wanting a piece of earth that answers to him before it answers to anyone else.

title: The king gives Ìomhar the river-grazing of the eastern marches
body: The king grants Ìomhar Dearg thin-soiled river-grazing between the last settled households and the open country to the east, telling him only that a share given is a share that can be taken back, as every share on the island has been and will go on being.

title: Ìomhar stands on his own ground looking east
body: At the day's end Ìomhar Dearg stands alone on the eastern river-grazing, thin grass under his own feet for the first time in nearly eight centuries of walking ground that answered to another name, and looks east toward country he has not yet walked.

title: Fields at Achadh mhòr
body: The wide field at Achadh mhòr, near the warm springs, is cleared and banked, the largest single field of the age. Its bank is laid with the stones of an older wall that no one claims.

title: Achadh mhòr's wide field is cleared under Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
body: A household near Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh clears and banks the widest single field the eastern country has yet cut from the rough, laying its bank on the stones of an older wall whose builders none of them can name, and grows in a good year wheat enough for three households where before there had been land for none.

title: An Cnoc Ruadh's boats come to be kept at Baile ghlas
body: Boats drawn up in stone and turf sheds at Baile ghlas along the lake shore come, within a generation, to put out oftener than An Cnoc Ruadh's own strand, so that the harbour built beside the hill grows quietly into the hill's chief fishing ground.

title: Achadh naomh fences its spring before it raises a house
body: Settlers at Achadh naomh lead a spring round in channels of their own digging and fence it before a single wall is raised, so that a stranger coming on the place first might take the water, and not the people, for what had been settled there.

title: The harbour at Baile ghlas
body: The households of the Red Hill draw up their boats at Baile ghlas, along the lake shore from the hill, in sheds of stone and turf. It becomes the fishing harbour of the Red Hill.

title: Two households at Caol shean give their disputed landing to no one
body: Rather than let a quarrel over a stretch of river landing run on with no keeper near enough to draw a lot on it, two households of Caol shean sit out a night together and give the ground to the landing itself, for whoever has a boat drawn up there and no other claim; the households are, within two generations, thoroughly mixed by marriage.

title: Achadh naomh's spring-fields
body: Settlers at Achadh naomh in the north water their fields from a spring they will not build over, and lead the water round it in channels. The spring is fenced before any house is.

title: Catrìona born of the king's blood
body: A daughter of the king's blood is born in the valleys under the hill and named Catrìona; before she is ten she can give a household's line back seven names, and the hill begins to watch her as a valley watches a child who does an ordinary thing early.

title: Caol gharbh on the rough strait
body: Households settle at Caol gharbh on the north-east coast and fish the strait in skin boats. They lay paddles beside their dead.

title: Doire chiar
body: A settlement grows up under the dark oaks at Doire chiar in the north. Its people pen pigs in the wood and drive them out to the acorns at the fall of the year.

title: The river landing at Caol shean
body: Caol shean, on the Abhainn ìseal east of the vein, becomes the river landing of the hill households of the east. Salt, fish and seal-skins come up the river to it from the coast, and go on from it into the keepers' country.

title: Ailis is born east of the vein
body: A girl named Ailis is born at what will become Dùn dhearg, into a household already turf-cutting for the fort's first bank, and grows up along the ditch's edge hearing, at her own hearth, tellings of a king beyond the vein who does not grow old.

title: A trader tells Ailis of the gate at Dùn ìseal
body: A cloth-trader passing through Caol shean's landing tells the children at a hearth of standing at the very gate of Dùn ìseal and seeing a young-faced man come in at it who has held that hill, by every account at the gate, since before its walls were built; the child Ailis asks whether it does not frighten his own children to grow old beside him, and gets no clear answer.

title: Dùn dhearg raised
body: A hill-fort with a double bank is raised at Dùn dhearg, east of the vein, by households who owe nothing to Dùn ìseal. The Stone Kings' list does not name its holders; it says only that Dùn dhearg came not to the gatherings.

title: The households east of the vein raise the double bank at Dùn dhearg
body: Owing nothing to Dùn ìseal and asking leave of no one, the households of the eastern country dig a deep ditch and raise a double bank at Dùn dhearg, sharing out the labour and afterward the ground within it by households and not by standing, so that the fort itself sets, without any law behind it, the custom the country keeps from then on.

title: A holdout household is left outside Dùn dhearg's second bank
body: A family that refuses to send hands to the digging is simply left with its grazing outside the second bank when the ground is drawn, and asks within a generation, of its own accord and under no compulsion, to be let in on the same terms as its neighbours, its late hands reckoned at somewhat less than hands sent early.

title: Gille-Brìde's father born in Na Glinn Àrda
body: A son is born in Na Glinn Àrda to a household of Somhairle's line, which keeps Sloinneadh a' Chlachair and takes no share; he will live three hundred and eight years, fewer than his own father, and father Gille-Brìde.

title: Ruairidh born to Dùghall mac Ìomhair
body: A son is born to Dùghall, son of Ìomhar Dearg, and named Ruairidh, grey-eyed like his great-grandfather the king; Ìomhar holds him at his naming and says the boy will outlive the river-grazing and most of what stands on it.

title: Ailis's husband is buried on the slope above Dùn dhearg
body: The net-mender of Caol shean whom Ailis married in her twenty-second year dies at Dùn dhearg an old man by any island's reckoning, and is carried out and laid on the slope above the houses with his own net-needle set in the ground at his feet.

title: Seumas born on An Cnoc Ruadh
body: A son is born in An Cnoc Ruadh's hall and named Seumas; the reciters of the lake shore mark his birth in the roll as they have marked every holder's since Beathag Ruadh.

title: Ailis sets out for the ford with seal-skins
body: In her eighty-first year Ailis of Dùn dhearg carries three winters' store of seal-skins the length of the island toward Cruinneachadh an Àtha, meaning to trade them for salt and to stand in the river of the old tellings before her legs fail her; six of that country go with her, the first of Dùn dhearg's people to make the journey.

title: Dùn dhearg comes to the ford
body: In the time of Catrìona Mhòr the households of Dùn dhearg come to the ford gathering for the first time, bringing seal-skins and asking for salt. They are given ground of their own on the far bank.

title: The east reaches the ford after five days on the road
body: Ailis's party finds households along the road who have never heard of the country east of the vein, and sleeps a night with a family whose grandfather claims a telling, four hands removed, of An Cruinneachadh Mòr held in the three-thousandth year of the Grove; by the fourth day they walk unremarked among a general traffic of salt- and wool-carriers bound the same way.

title: Ìomhar Dearg names the east 'the short-lived' at the ford
body: At the fire where Catrìona hears Ailis out, Ìomhar Dearg, holding river-grazing nearby, asks carelessly why ground should be troubled over for people who will all be dead within one of his own lifetimes, and calls them, in that breath, the short-lived; Ailis answers that she has five days' walking behind her and no wish to spend any of what time she has left arguing with a man who will have five centuries to be sorry in.

title: Young Catrìona gives Dùn dhearg ground at the ford
body: Catrìona, of the king's blood and not yet two hundred and twenty-five years old, hears Ailis of Dùn dhearg out at the ford, asks after the double bank and whether it answers to anyone, and gives the eastern households ground of their own on the far bank, this year and every year after, asking no oath in return and receiving none.

title: Salt is carried home to Dùn dhearg without any oath given
body: Ailis's party trades its seal-skins for salt enough to see three households through a hard winter and walks home east of the vein without having sworn anything to the ford or to the hill, and the elders of Dùn dhearg agree, hearing it told, that ground held and no word owed for the holding suits them exactly as it stands.

title: Settlers at Àth fhiadhaich
body: Households settle at Àth fhiadhaich in the south-eastern hills, by a ford where wild cattle cross. They take the calves and rear them, and their herds become the best in those hills.

title: Ailis dies on the slope above the double bank
body: Ailis dies at eighty-five in her own house on the eastern slope of Dùn dhearg's bank, three years after her one journey to the ford, and is buried beside her husband; her grandchildren keep the tale of the seal-skins and the woman of the king's blood who asked nothing back for the ground she gave.

title: The ford of the wild cattle is settled at Àth fhiadhaich
body: A household settles a stony crossing in the south-eastern hills where wild cattle come down to drink, and rears the calves born on the near bank apart from the wild herd until, within three generations, that ford's cattle are spoken of the length of the coast as the best in the hills.

title: Ceann àrsaidh
body: Households from the Red Hill settle the point at Ceann àrsaidh on the Abhainn fhionn. They find an old river landing there and name the place for it: the ancient headland.

title: Cnoc thais in the north-west
body: Households settle on the damp hill at Cnoc thais in the north-west and drain it with ditches. The ditches carry water still.

title: Inis mhòr
body: Households settle Inis mhòr on the Abhainn ghorm in the north-east and live by the fish of its sheltered pools. They build their houses in two rows facing each other, the oldest street on Dia-thìr.

title: Households build about the old landing at Ceann àrsaidh
body: People out of An Cnoc Ruadh's country find an old river landing on the Abhainn fhionn, stones set for a boat's keel by hands none living can name, and build their houses about it, naming the place for what they found.

title: Inis mhòr's two facing rows are raised
body: Households settle Inis mhòr on the Abhainn ghorm and build their houses in two rows facing each other across a single trodden way, so that a neighbour's fire may be borrowed without crossing open ground in the rain; it is the oldest street any teller remembers on Dia-thìr.

title: Baile gheal in the south-west
body: Baile gheal is founded on the south-western plain round a house with white-limed walls. The lime is burned from the shells of the old middens along the coast.

title: Àth bheag on the eastern coast
body: Households settle the small ford at Àth bheag on the far eastern coast, the easternmost dwelling of the age on the main island. Their boats go out after the geese on the islands.

title: Catrìona Mhòr
body: Catrìona Mhòr, twelfth of the Stone Kings and of the king's blood, holds Dùn ìseal under him; hers is the last name in the spoken list. It is told that she knew every household of the hills by its line seven names back.

title: Seumas Òg of the Red Hill
body: Seumas Òg holds the Red Hill, and with him the spoken list of the Red Hill ends. In the next age what the reciters kept of it is written down.

title: The two lists recited together
body: At the ford gathering, in the time of Catrìona Mhòr, the list of the Stone Kings and the list of the Red Hill are recited one after the other from the first name to the last. It takes from dusk to dawn. For the first time both are heard whole.

title: Catrìona takes the hill of Dùn ìseal
body: Catrìona, of the king's blood and two hundred and forty-seven years old, takes Dùn ìseal formally as the twelfth to hold it of Rìghrean na Cloiche' line, known already for a memory that can give any household's line back seven names without pausing to think.

title: Seumas Òg takes An Cnoc Ruadh
body: A young man of seven-and-twenty named Seumas takes up the holding of An Cnoc Ruadh his own line has kept since the palisade first burned, the same season Catrìona takes Dùn ìseal; his name will be the last An Cnoc Ruadh's own spoken roll carries.

title: The two rolls are spoken whole at the ford in one night
body: Eòin gives the whole roll of Rìghrean na Cloiche from Ailean Mòr to Catrìona's own name, and Ùna gives the whole roll of An Cnoc Ruadh from Beathag Ruadh to Seumas Òg's, from dusk to the grey before morning; it is the first time either roll is heard whole, and those nearest the king see him smile when his own name is spoken.

title: Lots drawn for the slab
body: The lot for the keeper of the slab is drawn now among households from every part of the hills, not only those near the crack. The keepers' house at Tobar dhìreach becomes a place of pilgrimage.

title: The lot for the slab is drawn from every part of the hills
body: Where the lot for the keeper of the slab was once drawn only from households near the crack, it comes in these years to be drawn from every part of the hills alike, and Tobar dhìreach becomes a place walked to for its own sake by households whose grandparents never heard the crack mentioned.

title: A nameless hand recuts Calbh Cnoc ghorm
body: A hand from Catrìona's own hill goes out to Calbh Cnoc ghorm and recuts its worn grooves along their old lines before the rain can lose them; some who come after hold that a single stroke changed in the recutting, though none can agree which, or prove any changed at all.

title: The keepers number nine
body: The keepers of the slab are made nine, one drawn by lot for each of nine districts of the hills. They meet at the slab when a keeper dies, and at no other time.

title: Luchd-faire na Lice settle at nine
body: The keepers settle at nine, one drawn by lot for each of nine districts of the hills that no household has ever marked on the ground but every household somehow knows the edge of; the nine meet at the slab only when one of their number dies.

title: Coal in every hearth by the handful
body: Every household of the hills burns its handful of the coloured coal, measured in a copy of the stone cup, on one night in the dark of the year, the night later kept as Samhain. All burn at once by agreement, so that the low fires of the handful show on every hillside on the same night.

title: A handful refused at Cnoc dhubh
body: The household of the Cnoc dhubh trench, where the two diggers were crushed, refuses its handful of coal for as long as any remembers. No household before it is known to have chosen not to burn at all.

title: The handful comes to be burned all at once by agreement
body: Without any lot or law behind it, every household in reach of another comes to burn its measured handful of an gual dathach on the same dark night, each watching for the first low flame on the nearest hill before lighting its own; the night comes to be called Oidhche na Glaice.

title: Cnoc na Claise's household refuses its handful
body: The descendants of Torcall Tochlair, who stayed by the trench where his brother was crushed, will not burn the handful with the rest of the hills and give no single answer twice for it; Catrìona sends no one to compel them, and none at the slab asks her to.

title: The cord of Dùn ìseal grows to nine hundred knots
body: Finding she can no longer carry the whole tally of households in her own head, Catrìona sets her people to counting them plainly on a knotted cord, a knot to a hearth, which grows through her years of holding to some nine hundred knots, the largest count made on Dia-thìr in the age; the king's own kin are never upon it.

title: Counting the households
body: The people of Catrìona Mhòr count the households of the hills by knots on a cord, a knot to a hearth. The cord of Dùn ìseal is said to have borne some nine hundred knots, the greatest count made on Dia-thìr in this age.

title: The saying on the column recut
body: The words on the column at Cnoc ghorm, worn shallow, are recut in their old grooves by a hand from the hill of the Stone Kings. Some later readers hold that the recutting changed a letter; none can prove which.

title: The tally stones of Seann Dunn are set back in their old order
body: A family digging a house-floor into an old midden at Seann Dunn strikes a row of upright stones each cut with a single stroke, knows them for the tally stones of the coast's old people, and sets them back as they lay rather than break them for the floor, building further along the midden's shoulder instead.

title: The last Seann-Dhaoine midden disturbed
body: Households at the eastern Seann Dunn cut into the old midden for a house-floor and find the tally stones. They put them back in the order they lay and build elsewhere.

title: The south-eastern coast rows its dead to Eilean ìseal
body: The custom grows along the south-eastern coast of rowing the newly dead out to Eilean ìseal rather than burying them on the mainland shore, whether learned from the old coast people's graves across the strait or come to of itself; the tellings let the question stand unsettled.

title: Eilean ìseal given to the dead
body: The households of the south-east coast begin to row their dead to Eilean ìseal, after the old manner of the Seann-Dhaoine. Whether they learned it from the Seann Vell graves on Eilean dhearg, or came to it of themselves, is not told.

title: Eilean chrom stays unfished
body: No household puts out a boat to fish the waters of Eilean chrom, where Gilleasbuig Beag was left with no boat to come back in; his fire was seen three nights running the first year and then no more, and the island stays empty and unfished.

title: Gilleasbuig Beag's island
body: Eilean chrom, where Gilleasbuig Beag was left, stays empty and unfished. His fire is seen on it for three nights, the tellings say, and then no more.

title: The keepers ask to be named
body: The nine keepers of the slab ask Catrìona Mhòr to declare their charge before the whole ford gathering, so that no king after her may draw the lot at Dùn ìseal. She neither refuses nor agrees, and the matter is left to the next age.

title: The nine keepers ask Catrìona to declare their charge
body: The nine of Luchd-faire na Lice come up together at the ford and ask Catrìona, then in her twenty-ninth year of holding, to declare their charge over the slab, the lot and the handful before the whole gathering so that no king after her may reach for it as Calum Ciar once did; she names the eldest of them by his own line before he finishes bowing.

title: Catrìona answers the keepers: not this year, ask me again
body: Catrìona gives the nine keepers neither refusal nor consent, telling them only, "Not this year," and then, before the eldest can press her further, "Ask me again"; the nine go back to their own fires by the slab to wait.

title: Eòin Beul-binn and Ùna Ruadh die within two years of each other
body: Eòin, whose voice carried the whole roll of Rìghrean na Cloiche across one night at the ford, dies in his eightieth year, and Ùna, who answered him roll for roll for An Cnoc Ruadh, follows him within two years in her seventy-third; the telling of that single night passes from then on at second hand.

title: Catrìona falls ill on the hill
body: In her two hundred and eighty-ninth year the sickness comes on Catrìona that will not leave again; she keeps her seat at Dùn ìseal as long as she is able, still able to give a household's whole line back seven names, and the nine keepers, hearing of it, send no word asking again.

title: Seumas Òg dies on An Cnoc Ruadh
body: Seumas Òg, the last name An Cnoc Ruadh's spoken roll carries, dies in his seventy-first year in the winter before Catrìona Mhòr, and the lake shore keeps no holder's fire for him after, only its own.

title: The king's kin bring their claims to the hill
body: After Catrìona Mhòr's death every soul of the king's blood within three days' walk comes to Dùn ìseal to press a claim on the hill, each able to say the two names of a line whose second name is always Ailean's; the king hears every claim with the same still face.

title: The king takes back the hill
body: Catrìona Mhòr dies, and with her the list of the Stone Kings ends. Her kin put forward many claims to Dùn ìseal, and Ailean Mòr gives the hill to none of them. He comes to it himself and holds it in his own hand, as in the first days.

title: The king holds the hill and gives it to none
body: The king tells the gathered claimants that no line among them is better than another and that Catrìona Mhòr's line cannot be handed to a stranger's open palm; he will hold the hill himself, as before Gormshuil first took it up in his name.

title: The first marriage reckoned openly for a share
body: A young man of a minor line is married to a woman three lines removed from the king, and his father says openly at the betrothal fire that the match is made to bring five lines instead of three nearer the front of the reckoning, should the king ever name an heir.

title: A daughters' claim disputed at a betrothal
body: A household holding good grazing but no claim of its own is joined by marriage to one that claims through four generations of daughters, and the hill argues without settling whether a claim run through daughters weighs more or less than one run through sons.

title: A betrothal broken over a nearer claim
body: A grandmother breaks off her granddaughter's marriage within the month of its making, having found a nearer claim on the groom's own side that she judges would weigh the match's worth downward; the hill takes it as proof that every marriage among the blood is now made for its shares and not for anything else.

title: A household of the western slopes loses its grazing
body: A household that has held grazing on the western slopes eleven generations is told, without reason given, to remove itself to ground of equal size two valleys over before winter; asked directly why, the king says only that a share given has always been a share that can be taken back.

title: Raonaid nic Ailein dies at the river-meadow
body: Raonaid nic Ailein, the king's daughter, dies at her own river-meadow in her one thousand three hundred and eightieth year; the king sits with her the better part of a day and a night, as he sat once with Gormshuil and once with Somhairle, and speaks of it to no one after.

title: The king takes back Raonaid's grazing
body: Within the month of Raonaid nic Ailein's burying the king sends word that the river-meadow grazing is wanted elsewhere and that Niall Òg, her nearest of that line, is to remove his household from it; Niall answers, as he has come to answer every such word, with a laugh.

title: Dùn dhearg will not bow
body: The king sends to Dùn dhearg and to the households east of the vein, bidding them come in to him. They send his messenger back with nothing, and swear among themselves that they will owe nothing to Dùn ìseal nor to its king. From that year the spears of the east are gathered at Dùn dhearg.

title: The king sends Niall Òg to Dùn dhearg
body: The king chooses Niall Òg to carry word east of the vein, bidding the households of Dùn dhearg come in to him at last, judging that a man known for asking nothing on his own account is less likely to be mistaken for the leading edge of a conquest.

title: Niall Òg finds Dùn dhearg wanting nothing of the hill
body: Niall Òg crosses the vein and finds the double bank of Dùn dhearg larger and better kept than any western telling had prepared him for, its forges and granary proof of a country that has gone far, by its own hands, toward needing nothing from Dùn ìseal.

title: Fearghal Donn refuses the king's asking
body: Fearghal Donn, holder of Dùn dhearg, hears the king's messenger before the whole household and answers that his people have raised their own bank and buried their own dead without any man's leave, and will not be counted among a kin who marry for shares and wait a thousand years for a hill never given.

title: Niall Òg carries the refusal home
body: Niall Òg rides back to Dùn ìseal and gives Fearghal Donn's word to the king plainly; the king says he had looked for no other answer, thanks him for the carrying of it, and turns to the next claim waiting for him.

title: The spears of the east are kept to hand
body: Word reaches Dùn ìseal by traders, not by any messenger sent for the purpose, that the households about Dùn dhearg have begun keeping their own spears closer than ever before, against a quarrel none of them will name; the king does nothing about it that anyone can see.

title: A woman of Clann na Ceiste speaks over the child
body: An old woman of Clann na Ceiste, come down from the slab to see the new child, tells Gille-Brìde that a boy born short-lived among the long-lived will learn early what his own kin have never needed to learn until late: how much of a life can be made to matter in however much of it is given.

title: Ceallach is born in Na Glinn Àrda
body: A son is born to Gille-Brìde of Somhairle's line in Na Glinn Àrda and is called Ceallach; he is slower to walk and to run than the children before him, the first sign, told back afterward, that the years were coming down faster in him than in his father.

title: The eve of the Binding
body: The handful is kept everywhere in the hills, the keepers are nine, the sharing before the storms is kept on every coast, and the saying is spoken at every gathering. None of it is yet declared, and no oath is yet sworn over the vein. The king holds Dùn ìseal in his own hand, his kin wait about him for their shares, and the spears of the east gather at Dùn dhearg.

title: Fearghal Donn dies at Dùn dhearg
body: Fearghal Donn, who had held Dùn dhearg since before Niall Òg was sent to him and sent back with nothing, dies an old man in his own bed at the fort; the households east of the vein bury him as they buried Ailis, without word sent to the hill and none expected back.

title: Artair takes up the holding of Dùn dhearg
body: Artair, Fearghal Donn's son, takes up the holding of Dùn dhearg with no more ceremony than his father had used, and says at the burying itself that he will hold what his father held and ask nothing further of the hill until the day it asks something of him.

title: Gille-Brìde's father dies in his three hundred and eighth year
body: Gille-Brìde's father dies at Samhain in his three hundred and eighth year, fewer years than his own father had, dying as most of that line has learned to die: without illness or wound, simply slower each year until one morning he does not rise from his own hearthstone.

title: Word runs that the kin will gather below Dùn ìseal
body: At the burying, word runs among the fires that the king's kin mean at last to come down out of their scattered holdings and gather in the valley below Dùn ìseal, each line with its own tents and its own fire, to wait together upon the shares left uncounted since Catrìona Mhòr's death.

title: The kin come down household by household
body: Through the summer the king's kin come down into the valley below Dùn ìseal household by household and line by line, no single word sent to call any of them, until the valley holds more tents and more fires than any one household has ever seen gathered in one place.

title: Murchadh Mòr brings his sons and grandsons down
body: Murchadh Mòr comes down from the northern plain with a column of sons and grandsons that takes three days to pass any one point on the road, carrying more tent-cloth, it is said, than the valley below Dùn ìseal has ever seen brought to one place at once.

title: Eithne's knot-keeper counts every soul on the new ground
body: Eithne comes down from below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire with her own household, and her knot-keeper walks at its head with the household's cord wound about his arm, meaning to be seen keeping count of every soul who sets foot on the new ground, and does so from the first day to the last.

title: Ìomhar Dearg pitches nearest the vein
body: Ìomhar Dearg comes down from the eastern marches nursing a hundred years' grievance over river-grazing he judges his by use if not by the king's word, and pitches his tents nearer the vein than any other line thinks wise, exactly, everyone agrees, like him.

title: Sìne nan Snaidhm keeps the cord of the whole valley
body: Sìne nan Snaidhm, knot-keeper of the household cord at Dùn ìseal, walks the growing valley of tents checking each new fire against the cord she carries, so that within a season no soul is pitched there, of the king's blood or of any household following it down, whose count she has not kept.

title: A steward is set over every line
body: By the second summer a steward stands over every line camped below Dùn ìseal, holding no ground and no lordship, only charged to speak for its household at the common fires and see its people fed and housed while the waiting goes on, until the valley looks less like a gathering than a town that never raised walls.

title: Sluagh an Ear begins to gather at Dùn dhearg
body: In the spring Sluagh an Ear begins gathering at Dùn dhearg under Artair, who is said to have waited three years, since he first took up his father's holding, for the very stillness of the hill to break; word of the gathering reaches the western fires within the week.

title: Gille-Brìde and Ceallach come down to see the valley
body: Gille-Brìde walks down out of Na Glinn Àrda with Ceallach, now grown but already, though neither says it, walking more slowly than a man of his years should, and the two stand at evening looking over more fires than either has ever seen gathered at once.

title: Sìne nan Snaidhm names Gille-Brìde the one soul asking nothing
body: Sìne nan Snaidhm tells Gille-Brìde that his name is on no cord she carries, since he has asked for no ground and no share from anyone, and that he is, that night, the only soul in the whole valley of whom that can be said.

title: The king goes down to meet the east with a handful of household
body: Near the end of summer the king comes down from Dùn ìseal with no more than three tents' worth of his own household, going to meet the east himself, while every line camped in the valley says, each at its own fire, that it will follow him within a day or two.

title: The king sends Gille-Brìde home to the hills
body: Gille-Brìde asks the king plainly whether he too should come down to the ford; the king tells him to go home to his own people instead, since whatever comes of it will want telling afterward by someone who was not in it, and his line has always been better at the telling than the coming.

title: The host of Dùn dhearg musters at the ford
body: Every household east of the vein sends its spears down to the river below Dùn dhearg in the last days of an Lùnastal, camping the whole night along a mile of the east bank under Artair mac Fhearghail, meaning to hold the crossing before the king's kin can gather against them.

title: Artair mac Fhearghail recalls the answer sent to the king
body: At the fires the first night, Artair mac Fhearghail repeats to the host the answer his father Fearghal Donn once sent back with the king's messenger, that the households east of the vein would keep their own bank and owed the hill at Dùn ìseal nothing, and says the answer has not changed in eighty years.

title: The east finds the king alone at the ford
body: At sunrise the host of Dùn dhearg finds a single man sitting on the stone at the head of the ford, his kin nowhere on the far bank; word runs down the fires that the king's own household has quarrelled over the shares of his kingdom and would not follow him east.

title: The first rush breaks on the king at the ford
body: Two hundred spears go into the ford together at sunrise on the first day and are thrown back with the king alone in the water among them; the host sees the river run red below the crossing before the morning mist has fully lifted.

title: The east tries the ford's edges and its throwing spears
body: Through the first day the host tries the deep channel above and below the ford to come at the king from the side, and by afternoon empties its fletchers' whole store throwing spears from the bank; neither the crossing nor the throwing turns him from his stone.

title: A household of Caol shean loses a man to the first day's ford
body: A net-mender's kinsman of Caol shean, twenty years unhurt at every boundary quarrel of the eastern country, goes into the first rush and is not seen to come out of the river; his wife asks after him at every fire down the bank until evening, then asks no more.

title: The dead of the host begin to dam the ford
body: On the second day the drowned and the slain lie so thick at the shallows below the crossing that the river backs up over the gravel, running warm and red, and the men of Dùn dhearg must climb their own dead to reach water shallow enough to cross.

title: The king draws a boy of Dùn dhearg from the river with his own hand
body: In the press of the second day the king takes the spear from the hands of a sixteen-year-old of the eastern host as a mother takes a knife from a child, and the boy is carried out alive on the east bank; the telling of that hand is kept by the east long after his name is forgotten.

title: Artair mac Fhearghail counsels the host to go in together
body: On the second night, with some of the host ready to go home, Artair mac Fhearghail tells the fires that the king is flesh and must have an end, as a cliff has an end before the sea, and counsels every spear of the east to go into the river together on the third day and not draw back.

title: The whole strength of the east goes into the river together
body: At first light on the third day every spear the east country has enters the ford at once and does not draw back, the host closing on the king from three sides the whole day long while the dead already in the water rise higher than the shallows had ever stood.

title: A light is seen on the water around the king
body: In the afternoon of the third day men near the middle of the ford see a light low along the river's surface where the king stands, of no colour any of them had a word for, and say afterward only that they saw every colour in it and none, and would say no more.

title: The king's kin fail to come to the ford
body: Through all three days at the ford below Dùn dhearg, no household of the king's own blood, and no spear of the hills, comes down the western track to stand with him; Sluagh an Ear has the river to itself the whole time.
